tools.name: Zotero
tools.blurb: A free tool from an independent nonprofit for collecting, organizing, annotating, citing and sharing what you read, running on Mac, Windows, Linux, iOS and Android, with a browser connector that senses a source as you browse and files it with its metadata, collections for broad sorting, tags for the threads that cross topics, and a search across keyword, author, publication and partial title that retires folder digging altogether, which is how XDA's Yash Patel stopped losing articles he had already read; the honest caveat is storage, because a free account syncs only 300MB before the paid tiers begin at $20 a year for 2GB and climb to $60 for 6GB and $120 for unlimited.

tools.name: Lumo by Proton
tools.blurb: A privacy-first AI assistant from Proton, the people behind Proton Mail and Proton VPN, which answers questions, researches the web with citations you can check, analyzes data, writes and generates images, stores every conversation under zero-access encryption Proton says it cannot read, never trains on your chats, publishes its code open source, leaves memory off by default so one conversation does not carry into the next, and adds a ghost mode for chats you would rather not keep; How-To Geek's Nimrah Chaudhry spent a week on it instead of ChatGPT and kept both tools, because the free tier caps messages, chat history, image generations and projects at one, the image quality trails its rivals, the brainstorming came back average, third-party integrations are thin, and a first answer usually needs a follow-up before it has any depth.

tools.name: OpenCut
tools.blurb: An open-source video editor that runs in a browser tab and exports MP4 or WebM with no watermark, using the browser's built-in WebCodecs encoding and a Rust compositor compiled to WebAssembly so the rendering leans on your own GPU, with drag-and-drop import, a timeline of one main video track plus organized secondary tracks, keyframe animation with a bezier curve editor, preset-shape masks with feather and stroke, auto-captioning and transcripts that detect multiple languages, more than a thousand fonts, loudness-weighted audio waveforms and single-frame PNG export for thumbnails, which is what sped XDA's Nolen Jonker up after CapCut; the caveats are substantial, because this is an early beta in the middle of a ground-up rewrite, transitions do not exist yet, the effects list stops at blur, projects live in the browser's own IndexedDB store so clearing site data destroys them, and nothing syncs between devices.

tools.name: F-Droid 2.0
tools.blurb: The free and open-source Android app repository, rewritten in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose after a year of work and 14 test releases into what the project calls its largest app update in 10 years, now built around Discover, Search and My Apps, with an expanded category system, a search that reaches into app descriptions, categories and translations, better support for Chinese, Japanese and Korean, and a unified installer that uses the new pre-approval APIs opened by the EU Digital Markets Act; the caveats are worth knowing before you go looking for it, because 2.0 arrives in a staged rollout rather than all at once, Android 6 devices and the F-Droid Privileged Extension are no longer supported, pull-to-refresh is gone in favor of automatic background updates, Tor auto-detection has been folded into generic proxy settings, and the Nearby file-sharing feature is still being finished.

tools.name: PowerToys FancyZones
tools.blurb: Microsoft's own window manager, part of the free PowerToys set: you draw zones on the screen once, then every window you drag snaps into one at full size, with a grid layout that splits and merges and resizes with the screen or a canvas layout whose zones can overlap, Win+Shift+backtick to open the editor, Win+PgUp and Win+PgDn to cycle the windows stacked in one zone, and Win+Ctrl+Alt plus a number to swap the whole layout; the honest caveat is that it does not take over Windows Snap by default, so you hold Shift while dragging until you turn on Override Windows Snap, and Microsoft's own compatibility list names applications it cannot zone at all, among them Citrix Workspace, VMware Workstation Player, TeamViewer and Parsec, while elevated windows such as Task Manager need PowerToys itself running as administrator.

tools.name: Tasks.org
tools.blurb: An open-source to-do list and reminders app with no ads, licensed under the GNU GPLv3, that syncs against Tasks.org, Google Tasks, DAVx5, CalDAV, EteSync or DecSync CC and lines up with Outlook, Thunderbird and Apple Reminders, which is how How-To Geek's Joe Fedewa folded both Google Tasks and Google Keep into it, keeping lists or tags, start and due dates, priorities, subtasks, reminders, calendar entries and the location based Places reminders Keep no longer offers, with two way sync carrying new tasks back into Google Tasks for Google Home speakers and Gemini to read; the caveat is reach, because this is an Android app first, the desktop build is still alpha, and a household on iPhones gets nothing out of it.

tools.name: Portmaster
tools.blurb: Safing's free, open-source application firewall, which watches every connection the machine makes and shows you which program made it, then lets you block a single connection, a domain, a connection type, a country or an app's internet access altogether, with the free tier listing the privacy filter, secure DNS, the network monitor, network history, bandwidth visibility and weekly reports, and paid Plus at 40 euro a year or Pro at 8 euro a month and 80 euro a year adding investigation tools, priority support and the SPN across up to five devices; the caveat is the boundary, because it defends only the computer it is installed on, which is why How-To Geek's Dibakar Ghosh calls it a Honda Civic next to Pi-hole's Ford F-250, and turning on the broader filter lists can break sites you actually wanted.

tools.name: Candy Browser
tools.blurb: A gesture-first Android browser that runs Mozilla's GeckoView by default, so Firefox extensions such as uBlock Origin install and run on a phone, with a switch to the Android System WebView engine for sites that render better on Chromium, a Safari-inspired interface built for mobile, link previews, grid, list or Coverflow tab views, and filtering, history, favorites and profiles kept on the device, installable from Google Play, F-Droid, Obtainium or the project's own GitHub releases; the caveats are age and reach, since this is a young project at roughly 450 GitHub stars that needs Android 13 or newer, and Android Police's Dhruv Bhutani stops short of calling it a full Chrome or Firefox replacement.

tools.name: Ente Photos
tools.blurb: An open-source, end-to-end encrypted place to put photos and videos, with automatic backup, shared albums, public links and on-device AI across Android, iOS, the web, Mac, Windows and Linux, and 10GB free forever; the honest caveat is the size of that free tier, because a camera roll of any age runs past 10GB and lands you on a paid plan that starts at $2.49 a month for 50GB.

tools.name: Greenshot
tools.blurb: A free, open-source capture tool that takes a region, a window or a full screen, opens it in its own editor for annotating, highlighting or obfuscating the part you would rather not send, then exports in one step to a file, the clipboard, a printer, an email or Word, Excel, Outlook and OneNote, with filename patterns that stamp every capture with its time and title; the caveat is platform, because the free build is Windows only, currently 1.3.315 from March 20, while the Mac edition is a $1.99 App Store purchase.

tools.name: OSS Document Scanner
tools.blurb: A phone camera turned into a document scanner, with OpenCV enhancing the captured page, Tesseract reading the text off it, PDF export for sending it on, and barcode reading, free under an MIT license on both Android and iOS, which is why XDA's Mahnoor Faisal named it the open-source answer to Adobe Acrobat; the honest caveat is scale, because this is a volunteer project at roughly 2,500 GitHub stars with 82 issues open, so the polish trails the paid scanners.

tools.name: Default Launcher
tools.blurb: An Android home screen built on the AOSP Launcher3 code from Android 16 and restyled in Material 3, with a grid you can set anywhere from four to ten columns, icon shapes including circles, squares, arches, and cookies, folders that take an emoji as their cover instead of a collage of app icons, stacked widgets, and one search bar that finds apps, contacts, calendar entries, and files and doubles as a calculator, unit converter, and timezone converter, with the web and AI search providers left for you to pick rather than locked to Google; the project makes no internet connections and carries no telemetry and no tracking, keeping its data on the handset, and the honest catch is how you get it, since it is not on the Play Store and has to be sideloaded from the GitHub releases page, where Play Protect is likely to object the first time, and MakeUseOf's Oluwademilade Afolabi is clear that it is not trying to clone every Pixel flourish.

tools.name: PhotoRec
tools.blurb: A recovery program that ignores the file system entirely and carves data straight off the storage by hunting for known file signatures, which is why it still finds pictures when a card or drive reports itself as empty or unreadable, working across FAT, NTFS, exFAT, ext2 through ext4, and HFS+ on hard disks, CDs, USB sticks, and memory cards, and recognizing more than 480 file extensions across roughly 300 file families; it comes in the same download as TestDisk, and the limits are the price of the method, because MakeUseOf's Afam Onyimadu pulled 104,754 files off one drive and got no folder structure and no original filenames, just generic names like f123456789.jpg with thumbnails, duplicates, and broken fragments mixed in, TRIM on an SSD can put deleted data out of reach entirely, and the first rule the documentation gives is to stop writing anything else to the device.

tools.name: Radius
tools.blurb: A Meetup alternative for groups, events, and activities, where you browse or start a group across categories like arts, food and drink, science and technology, or gaming, schedule events for the people who join it, and post an activity, a lightweight note that you are doing something soon and would like company, which needs no group behind it at all, with the site offering a group set up in sixty seconds for free; the honest caveat is the one every young network carries, that a local directory is only as useful as the people already near you, and its hyper-local discovery is still marked BETA, so look up your own area before you plan an evening around it.

tools.name: OpenStock
tools.blurb: An open-source market tracker from the Open Dev Society that gives you watchlists, price alerts, company profiles, emailed summaries, and a command-palette search with no subscription anywhere in it, built on Next.js with Finnhub supplying the data and TradingView drawing the charts, and set up either through its Docker Compose file or through the project's own hosted instance; the caveats matter more than usual on this one, because the documentation says outright that market data may be delayed under provider rules, with international quotes running 15 minutes or more behind on free plans and TradingView's free tier restricted on some emerging markets, and the hosted instance is a community deployment that asks you to create an account, so give it a password you use nowhere else and treat it as a watchlist rather than as anything you would trade on.

tools.name: Harbor
tools.blurb: A notes app built to hold the messy half of a filing cabinet, with scans, photos, PDFs, audio recordings, and handwriting all searchable through OCR and transcription, a one step Evernote import that carries notebooks, tags, checklists, and attachments across, optional zero knowledge encryption per note or notebook, offline access, a web clipper, and an API, CLI, and MCP endpoint for connecting your own AI tools; the pricing page makes two promises worth holding it to, that the rate will not rise for three years and is then capped at ten percent a year, and that if you stop paying the account goes read only rather than being deleted, and it is candid about the one number a careful reader wants, since it says the free plan's exact limits are still being finalized for launch and only promises enough room to try an import of a notebook or two.

tools.name: Ditto
tools.blurb: An extension to the Windows clipboard that keeps everything you copy in a local database rather than the 25 item ceiling the built in history stops at, with search across the whole history, a small editor for fixing text before you paste it, a hotkey on Ctrl and backtick, and survival across restarts; MakeUseOf's Oluwaseun Bamisile set his retention to 200 entries and chose how long older ones live before they expire, and the project is plain that there is no login, no cloud service, and no telemetry, which is also where the limits sit, because Windows is the only platform it runs on, and a clipboard that remembers everything also remembers whatever you copied out of a password manager, until you clear it.

tools.name: FUTO Keyboard
tools.blurb: An Android keyboard that runs fully offline on the principle that a keyboard has no business connecting to the internet, with its own FUTO Swipe gesture typing, autocorrect and prediction, custom themes, and a companion voice input tool that transcribes without sending or storing anything; How-To Geek's Tyler Dupont counts it among the Gboard alternatives worth trying for its local voice typing, larger clipboard, and downloadable prediction models, and two limits belong on the label, that the project's own site warns it is still under active development and you may hit missing features or languages, and that the offline voice input comes as its own companion tool alongside the keyboard rather than as one download.

tools.name: Immich
tools.blurb: A self hosted photo and video library that behaves like the cloud service you are paying for, with a mobile app that backs the camera roll up in the background, duplicate detection, and search by person, place, date, or what is actually in the picture; MakeUseOf's Afam Onyimadu runs it on a recycled computer and makes the important distinction out loud, that Immich is the organizing layer while the original files stay on storage he controls, so he runs BorgBackup separately for the photos and videos and keeps database dumps for the metadata, and the honest cost is the part nobody advertises, because the project's own readme tells you to follow a 3-2-1 backup plan and self hosting hands you the drives, the electricity, the failures, and the maintenance.

tools.name: Lumiko
tools.blurb: A Chrome extension that records your screen and then adds the cinematic zoom and pan that normally takes an editor, following the cursor on its own, with a smart blur for anything sensitive on screen, a draggable webcam overlay, and a timeline you can still edit afterward; recording and export both run locally in the browser rather than in the cloud, and the honest catch is that free exports stop at 1440p and carry a Made with Lumiko badge, with clean video and full 4K reserved for the $9 one time Pro.

tools.name: VoiceCap
tools.blurb: A notetaker that either joins your Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, or Webex call or records the room from the phone in your pocket, then hands back a transcript with the speakers identified, a summary, and an action list you can search later and export as Markdown or plain text, with audio and transcripts held in EU data centers and kept out of model training; two limits are worth saying out loud, that the free tier stops at 300 minutes a month before the 29 euro Pro seat starts, and that whether you may record at all depends on the consent rules where you live, so tell the room first.

tools.name: Moda
tools.blurb: A browser design tool that turns a written brief into a slide deck, asking clarifying questions before it generates and then handing back real editable objects on a canvas rather than a flat picture, with export to PDF, PowerPoint, Google Slides, PNG, JPG, MP4, or GIF; XDA's Nolen Jonker got a six slide deck in under two minutes, and the ceiling is the thing to check before you rely on it, because the official pricing page puts the free plan at 500 AI credits per seat each month with decks capped at 10 slides.

tools.name: Mushotoku
tools.blurb: An Android app that keeps a calendar, tasks, habits, Markdown notes, journaling, mood tracking, and personal finance in one place, with each module switched on only if you actually want it, no account to create, no streaks to protect, and no internet permission built in at all, so the data stays encrypted on the handset; version 1.4 landed on July 26, 2026 and needs Android 13 or newer, and the catch is the same thing that makes it private, since fully offline means no sync between your devices and no cloud copy, leaving the backups to you.

tools.name: Trilium Notes
tools.blurb: A hierarchical note application that files everything into one deep tree, clones a single note into several branches at once, encrypts per note, and syncs to a server you host, with a README claim of scaling upwards of 100,000 notes; MakeUseOf's Jack Mitchell switched to it from Notion and states the catch plainly, that it looks decidedly plain out of the box and getting a workspace you enjoy takes theming and CSS you write yourself.

tools.name: Toolkit Tiles
tools.blurb: An open-source Android app that drops more than 30 small tools into the Quick Settings panel, among them a compass, a bubble level, a lux meter, caffeine mode, auto brightness, a screenshot tile, a clipboard cleaner, a DNS switch, and an SOS morse flashlight; the project warns that tile availability and behavior vary by device and Android version, and Android Police's Jon Gilbert found the Temperature tile refused to work and the Level stopped after a few seconds on a Pixel 10 Pro while both ran fine on a Galaxy Tab S9 FE.

tools.name: Firefox 156
tools.blurb: The September 15 release states that Firefox's built-in PDF viewer now starts up to 45% faster, adds a macOS option to launch the browser at login from the Startup section of settings, and fixes image dragging in rich-text editors, FLAC playback, Picture-in-Picture subtitles, and DNS over HTTPS connectivity; the honest caveat is that this is an update rather than a new app, so the gain only reaches you after the browser actually updates.

tools.name: LibreWolf
tools.blurb: An independent build of Firefox, made from the latest stable Firefox source, that ships with harder tracking and fingerprinting protection, telemetry removed, and DRM disabled; How-To Geek's Rich Hein keeps it for banking, shopping, and sensitive documents rather than the TV-connected machine, because by default it clears all cookies and site data, so staying signed in means whitelisting a site, Netflix needs DRM permission granted by hand, and WebGL takes configuration.

tools.name: KeePassXC
tools.blurb: An offline password manager that holds usernames, passwords, URLs, attachments, and notes in one encrypted database file on your own machine, with no account, no ads, no trackers, and no cloud service behind it; MakeUseOf names it the free replacement for the $35.88 a year 1Password Individual plan and states the catch in the same breath, that you back up and sync that file yourself and no provider can recover it for you.

tools.name: Edge Drop
tools.blurb: A clipboard manager that parks a slim bar at the edge of the screen and opens into a shelf holding everything you have copied, text, links, images, screenshots, and files, as cards you can preview, pin, delete, or drag straight into another app, installed from GitHub releases or the Microsoft Store; the caveats are that it is Windows only, a stack holds at most ten items, and there is no account and no cloud sync, so the history stays on that one machine.

tools.name: Hister
tools.blurb: A private search engine over the pages you have visited and the files you keep, indexing the full contents rather than titles and URLs so the half-remembered article comes back from a web page, a terminal, or an assistant you connect, and it sat on the Hacker News front page today at 348 points; the caveat is that you run and maintain it yourself, as a single local binary, Docker, or Nix, and optional semantic search sends text to whatever embeddings endpoint you configure.

tools.name: Duplicati 2.4
tools.blurb: It encrypts and compresses each incremental backup on your machine before sending it to S3, Backblaze B2, OneDrive, an SFTP server, or an external drive; the caveat is that you own the passphrase and Duplicati cannot reset it for you, so a lost phrase means a lost backup.

tools.name: Voiskey
tools.cost: Free to start, paid Pro tier
tools.blurb: It turns dictation into finished text across your apps in more than 100 languages, cleaning up fillers and changes of mind as you speak; the caveat is that the official site publishes no pricing at all, and the paid Pro tier above the free start appears only on the Product Hunt listing.

tools.name: Tinycast
tools.blurb: One hotkey opens app launching, clipboard history, file search, a calculator, snippets, and window management from a native Swift app with no third-party dependencies and no telemetry; the caveat is that it wants macOS 26, needs Accessibility permission to paste, and ships snippets turned off.

tools.name: Nextcloud
tools.blurb: Files, photos, calendar, contacts, mail, and real-time document editing run from a machine you own, with clients for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS; the caveat is that nobody else is keeping a spare copy, so plan redundant storage and one separate backup before you cancel anything.

tools.name: Stirling PDF 2.0
tools.kind: Desktop app or your own server
tools.blurb: An open source PDF workbench of more than 50 tools, merge, split, sign, redact, convert, OCR, and compress, installed as a Windows .exe, a macOS app, or a Linux .jar with no account, and version 2.0 adds a workspace that keeps one file open through several operations plus a text editor that MakeUseOf's Tashreef Shareef calls early access, good on plain letters and resumes and unreliable on scanned pages, tables, and multi-column layouts.

tools.name: RethinkDNS
tools.blurb: A DNS based blocker and firewall that filters ads, trackers, and malware across every app on an Android phone rather than inside one browser, with encrypted DNS over HTTPS or DNS over TLS and a choice of more than 190 blocklists, though Android Police's Rahul Naskar notes it claims the phone's single VPN slot, so an ordinary VPN cannot run beside it, and no blocklist stops every ad on the internet.

tools.name: Syncthing
tools.blurb: Keeps folders continuously in sync between your own computers with no cloud service in the middle and no central server holding your files, every transfer wrapped in TLS with forward secrecy, but XDA's João Carrasqueira points out that two machines only exchange changes while both are awake, which is why he leaves a spare laptop running as an always on relay.

tools.name: Oats
tools.blurb: A meeting notetaker that listens through your own computer rather than joining the call as a bot, transcribes on the device, labels who spoke, and blends your rough notes into a clean write up, with local Whisper and Ollama working out of the box and optional keys for Claude, Gemini, or OpenAI stored on your machine, though the Windows build is not code signed and throws a security warning the first time you open it.

tools.name: OpenDisplay
tools.blurb: Turns an iPhone or iPad you already own into a real second display for a Mac, extending the desktop rather than mirroring it, over the charging cable or Wi-Fi with no account and no dongle, at HiDPI resolution with touch input and hardware video encoding, though it leans on a private macOS display interface that an Apple update could break, the iPhone and iPad side arrives through TestFlight rather than the App Store, and audio forwarding is out of scope for now.

tools.name: Mozilla Thunderbird
tools.blurb: An open source mail client that gathers several accounts into one unified inbox, sorts arriving mail into folders by rule, searches across every account and folder at once, and keeps messages and attachments readable offline, with no ads in the inbox and no training of AI on your conversations, though MakeUseOf found it dated in use: menu placement is unintuitive, filters apply per account rather than globally, and it wants a setup session before it pays off.

tools.name: Notion
tools.blurb: A note editor built out of blocks instead of pages, where typing a slash command inserts checkboxes, tables, or collapsible toggles and a block that is converted keeps its old state if you switch it back, but the free plan holds file uploads to 5MB each and page history to seven days, and How-To Geek clocks the desktop app at roughly five to ten seconds to open against Word's under a second, plus a real learning curve at the start.

tools.name: Dolby On
tools.blurb: A free recording app that puts noise reduction, dynamic EQ, stereo widening, compression, de-essing, and volume maximization over whatever your phone microphone picks up, with six presets, noise and tone sliders, trimming, and 48kHz 16-bit WAV capture, though MakeUseOf is blunt that it is no substitute for a studio setup and that a noisy room still records as a noisy room.

tools.name: Memos
tools.blurb: A self-hosted timeline for short notes that takes Markdown, hashtags, and cross-references, adds a Chrome and Firefox web clipper, stores everything in SQLite on hardware you control, and sends no telemetry, but the documented quick start is a Docker command and a browser pointed at localhost:5230, about five minutes of work by MakeUseOf's account, rather than an app you simply install.

tools.name: Raycast 2.0
tools.blurb: A keyboard launcher that folds clipboard history, snippets, quicklinks, a calculator, and window management behind one shortcut with thousands of extensions on top, though the free plan keeps only three months of clipboard history and leaves Raycast AI to the paid Pro tier.

tools.name: Adobe Express
tools.blurb: Adobe's free plan costs nothing and needs no credit card, running in a desktop browser or on a phone with 5GB of storage and 10 days of version history, and MakeUseOf reports using it for highlights, shadows, saturation, warmth, sharpness, cropping, and background removal, while warning it is not the place for detailed masking, color grading, lens corrections, or RAW files.

tools.name: LocalSend
tools.blurb: An open source app that sends photos, videos, and documents straight to a nearby device over encrypted HTTPS with no account, no login, and no cloud upload, which XDA offers as the cure for emailing files to yourself, though every device has to sit on the same Wi-Fi network and it is built for immediate transfers rather than ongoing sync or remote recipients.

tools.name: Relic
tools.blurb: A clipboard manager that keeps everything you copy and syncs it under end to end encryption with a key the company says only you hold, capturing automatically on desktop and by share sheet on a phone, but the free tier holds only your last 500 copies plus 25 pinned items across three devices and 250 MB.

tools.name: Joplin
tools.blurb: An open source notebook that holds text, images, PDFs, and web clippings behind end to end encryption and runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS, though syncing means supplying your own Dropbox, OneDrive, or Nextcloud account or paying for Joplin Cloud, which starts at 2.99 euros a month, and Android Police calls the interface dated next to newer rivals.

tools.name: Audacity
tools.blurb: Free and open source recording and editing that converts between WAV, MP3, FLAC, and Ogg and accepts VST3 and Nyquist plugins, which is enough for recording, trimming, and converting everyday audio, but How-To Geek puts it about ninety percent of the way there for basic tasks rather than a full digital audio workstation.

tools.name: Fossify File Manager
tools.blurb: A file manager from the open source Fossify suite that carries no ads and no tracking libraries and asks only for the permissions its features need, though Android Police notes it stays focused on local storage and does not reach your cloud accounts.

tools.name: Ventoy
tools.blurb: Ventoy turns one USB stick into a boot menu by letting you copy ISO, WIM, IMG, VHDx, and EFI files straight onto the drive instead of reformatting for each one, but setting it up wipes the stick first, and MakeUseOf warns that some older rescue images still refuse to start without turning Secure Boot off.

tools.name: Super Productivity
tools.blurb: Open source and free forever, it holds tasks, a time tracker, a Pomodoro timer, and Kanban and Eisenhower boards in one offline app, though keeping devices in step means setting up your own WebDAV server or Dropbox sync.

tools.name: Bitwarden
tools.blurb: Basic password management stays always free and Premium adds an integrated authenticator, file attachments, and emergency access for $1.65 a month billed annually at $19.80, but as How-To Geek puts it, a cloud vault still lives on someone else's servers.

tools.name: Listary
tools.blurb: It reads the NTFS Master File Table directly to return file results in milliseconds and adds a folder jump inside Save and Open dialogs, and the free version is described as one hundred percent free, though its homepage never says what the paid Pro version costs.

tools.name: Winhance
tools.blurb: This open source utility strips preinstalled Windows apps and features from an ordinary window instead of a command line and can write tasks that re-remove them when an update puts them back, but some apps and features cannot be reinstalled after removal, so take the restore point it offers first.

tools.name: OBS Studio
tools.blurb: Free and open source recording and live streaming, now at version 32.2.2, handles a screen walkthrough for a colleague as readily as a broadcast, though How-To Geek's one fair complaint is that packing that much capability into a streamlined interface is hard.

tools.name: Alt-Tab Terminator
tools.blurb: Alt-Tab Terminator from NTWind replaces the built in Windows switcher with a vertical list of every open window, each carrying a large live preview, and it supports all versions of Windows from 7 to 11. How-To Geek's Tony Phillips, writing on September 9, types part of a window title to filter the list instantly, clicks an application icon to see only that app's windows, and scrolls the wheel while holding Alt rather than tapping Tab. The honest caveat is what the free edition leaves out: multi monitor support, custom hotkeys, window exclusion rules, and appearance customization all sit behind the Pro license, which the vendor lists at $19.95 or less for a lifetime.

tools.name: Pinta
tools.blurb: Pinta describes itself as a free, open source program for drawing and image editing, running on Linux, Mac, Windows, and BSD with select, crop, rotate, and resize alongside clone, recolor, and magic wand, live previews on effects and adjustments, and unlimited undo. How-To Geek's Goran Damnjanovic, writing on September 9, names it the replacement for Microsoft Paint in a set of four minimalist apps that displace cluttered Windows defaults. That framing is also the caveat: Pinta is pitched at Paint's territory, everyday photo work, digital painting, and pixel art, so anyone who needs a professional production suite will still open something larger.

tools.name: Jan
tools.blurb: Jan is an open source alternative to ChatGPT that its repository says runs 100% offline on your computer, downloading models from Hugging Face and, when you want them, reaching out to cloud providers from the same window; it is Apache 2.0 licensed and available for Windows 10 and later, macOS 13.6 and later, and most Linux distributions. XDA's Samarveer Singh, writing on September 9, values the workspace built around the models, the OpenAI compatible endpoint, and the built in web search more than raw speed. The caveats are hardware and candor about that speed: the project asks for 8GB of RAM for a 3B model, 16GB for 7B, and 32GB for 13B, and Singh writes that Jan does not run models dramatically faster than Ollama, which he still recommends for lightweight inference and automation.

tools.name: TinyRetroPad
tools.blurb: TinyRetroPad is a Notepad style Windows text editor of roughly 2,476 bytes, written in assembly and still carrying a full File, Edit, Format, View, and Help menu with open and save dialogs, find and replace, font selection, and printing. How-To Geek's Goran Damnjanovic, writing on September 9, places it among four minimalist replacements for Windows defaults, noting that it weighs less than 3KB and requires no sign in, installation, or account creation. Two caveats ride along: the repository warns that programs compressed with Crinkler can be flagged as a false positive by antivirus software including Windows Defender, and the project states plainly that it comes with no warranties and no guarantees.

tools.name: LibreOffice 26.8
tools.blurb: LibreOffice bundles Writer, Calc, Impress, Draw, Base, and Math into a single free download, and the 26.8 release adds a Paragraph Composer for justification, OpenType font variation support, calculated fields in Calc pivot tables, preservation of Microsoft Office chart types, multiple page sizes inside one document, and presentation sections in Impress. The honest caveat is fit rather than price. Writing in MakeUseOf on September 7, Tashreef Shareef found Calc without Power Query and newer functions such as LAMBDA, no real-time collaboration or cloud sync, font mismatches when opening PowerPoint files that installing Microsoft fonts mostly resolved, and a styles system in Writer that felt rough. If your work depends on live co-editing in a shared document, keep the subscription; if it does not, this replaces it tonight.

tools.name: UniGetUI
tools.blurb: UniGetUI puts one graphical front end on the command line package managers a Windows machine can already reach, covering WinGet, Scoop, Chocolatey, PowerShell, npm, Bun, pip, Cargo, .NET Tool, and vcpkg, so finding, installing, and updating software stops being ten separate errands; MakeUseOf's Oluwademilade Afolabi, writing on September 8, points to bulk updates with selective control, package pinning and version skipping, and Package Bundles that carry a saved set of apps onto a new machine. Two caveats ride along. The project states plainly that it is not affiliated with the package managers it integrates with and that packages are provided by third parties, so review sources and publishers before installing, and its maintainers warn that the only official site is devolutions.net/unigetui, because lookalike domains are circulating.

tools.name: Mailspring
tools.blurb: Mailspring is a free desktop mail client that gathers Gmail, iCloud, Office 365, FastMail, Outlook.com, Yahoo, and any IMAP or SMTP account into one window on Mac, Windows, and Linux, with native ARM64 and Wayland builds, and a Pro tier at $8 a month adds read receipts, link tracking, send later, follow-up reminders, templates, and unlimited snoozing. Read the caveats before you switch: the free version limits snoozing, reminders, and send later, the project describes a full calendar as coming later this year, and MakeUseOf's Tashreef Shareef, writing on September 7, hit login errors on Google accounts that required a manually created app password and found the app lagging when he moved between larger mailboxes.

tools.name: AntennaPod
tools.blurb: AntennaPod is an open source Android podcast manager that subscribes to any RSS feed, downloads episodes for offline listening, and keeps your listening under your own control rather than a recommendation engine's. Android Police's Marvin Velasco, writing on September 8, sets the feed refresh interval, which defaults to 12 hours, switches on global automatic downloads across every subscription, lets finished episodes delete themselves, arranges a home page from the queued, new, and downloaded lists, syncs subscriptions through independent providers, and exports an OPML file so leaving is easy. The caveat is who stands behind it: this is Android only, and the project says it is developed by volunteers without commercial backing, so there is no company support desk when something breaks.

tools.name: DaVinci Resolve
tools.blurb: Blackmagic's DaVinci Resolve 21.1 release reached the Hacker News front page on September 8, and the reason the tool belongs on a shelf rather than in a news column is the free edition, which Blackmagic describes as combining editing, color correction, visual effects, motion graphics, audio post production, and now photo editing in one application on Mac, Windows, and Linux. The free version works with 8-bit video up to 60 frames per second at resolutions as high as Ultra HD, 3840 by 2160, and includes multi-user collaboration and HDR grading. The caveat is where that ceiling sits: 10-bit video, frame rates to 120, resolutions beyond 4K, the AI Neural Engine, noise reduction, magic mask, and text-based editing all belong to DaVinci Resolve Studio at $295, which is a one-time purchase rather than a subscription.

tools.name: AppControl
tools.blurb: AppControl is a free Windows replacement for Task Manager whose real difference is memory: instead of showing only what a process is doing this second, it keeps days of CPU, GPU, and memory activity, with temperature history alongside, so you can scroll back to the moment something started straining the machine. It describes running processes in plain language, lets you disable an app, block a publisher, or write a custom rule, and raises an alert when an app reaches your webcam, microphone, or location, with the option to block or investigate. The current download is version 1.4.0.415 at 20.2 MB. Two caveats are worth carrying in: the makers say they built it as a tool they wanted for themselves and plan to offer optional premium features someday in the future, so free today is not a promise about every future feature, and XDA's Yash Patel, who wrote it up on September 7, is candid that it "didn't magically make my PC faster" and only made the diagnosis clearer, while warning against switching off components you do not understand. The AI tie-in is opt-in and separate: an open-source MCP extension that hands system data to a tool like Claude, Cursor, Gemini, OpenAI, or Windsurf, off by default.

tools.name: Firefox Focus
tools.blurb: Firefox Focus is Mozilla's stripped-down mobile browser, free on Android and iOS, and it treats privacy as the default rather than a mode you have to remember: Mozilla says it "blocks a wide range of common trackers by default including social trackers and those sticky ones that come from things like Facebook ads", and a single erase button on the search field clears your history, passwords, and cookies. The practical side effect Mozilla claims is speed, since pages stripped of trackers "require less data and load much faster". Android Police's Marvin Velasco, writing on September 5, describes a radical simplicity that quietly made it his default browser, with blocking on automatically and the session cleared on exit. The caveats are the design itself, and they are real: no browsing history, no extensions, no syncing between devices, four bookmarks reachable only at startup, and basic tabs with no real multitasking, plus the occasional search engine that answers permanent private mode with a CAPTCHA. Velasco says plainly that this should not be your only browser if you need bookmarks or a session that survives.

tools.name: OpenWhispr
tools.blurb: OpenWhispr calls itself the open source and free alternative to WisprFlow and Granola, and in ordinary use it means a global hotkey that drops spoken words straight into whatever field the cursor is in, plus transcription of audio files and recorded meetings with speaker labels, notes with semantic search, and dictation translation. The license is MIT and the project describes it as free for personal and commercial use. Two things are worth knowing before you install it: on Intel Macs live speaker identification and voice fingerprinting are unavailable, because ONNX Runtime no longer ships x86_64 binaries, so semantic search there falls back to keyword matching, and while local models cover every core feature, the optional cloud providers the app supports are separate services you would be signing up for yourself. It is listed on GitHub's daily trending page this afternoon with 7,286 stars, 225 of them gained today.

tools.name: NoSignups
tools.blurb: NoSignups is a directory of more than 200 open source tools that run in a browser tab and do not ask for an account or an email address first, sorted into productivity, design, development, writing, privacy, utilities, data, media, and education. It is live at nosignups.net, the directory code is GPL-3.0, and there is nothing to pay. The honest caveat is that this is a signpost rather than a product: each listed tool keeps its own license and its own quality, the project explicitly does not claim ownership of them, and every entry is described in 140 characters or fewer, so you still have to open a tool to judge it. It is listed on GitHub's daily trending page this afternoon with 3,267 stars, 436 of them gained today.

tools.name: Olauncher
tools.blurb: Olauncher replaces the Android home screen with a text list and no app icons, which is the entire point: the project describes itself as a minimal, ad-free launcher meant to cut screen time, it is GPLv3 with 3.8k stars, and it is free on both Google Play and F-Droid. Android Police's Marvin Velasco, writing on September 6, pins up to eight apps on the home screen, opens chosen apps with left and right swipes, and reaches everything else through an upward swipe into a searchable drawer, and he reports a drop in his own social media use, with apps like Reddit becoming less accessible and sometimes forgotten entirely. The caveats are real and he names them: the free version has no widget support, which he calls an unfortunate omission for productivity, the daily wallpapers are not dark-theme friendly, and anything you did not pin takes several deliberate taps. Widgets, weather, and folders live in the separate paid Pro Launcher, and the developer notes that some features are deliberately hidden in settings to keep the launcher simple.

tools.name: Kado
tools.blurb: Kado is a habit tracker that throws out the streak, scoring each habit with an exponential moving average instead, so that, as the project puts it, one missed day does not wipe your progress and you see a trend rather than a fragile chain. It handles yes-or-no habits, counters, and timers, schedules them daily, a set number of days per week, on chosen weekdays, or every few days, adds home screen and lock screen widgets with Siri and Shortcuts, and exports and imports your history as CSV or JSON so the data stays yours. Version 1.7 is shipping on the App Store, the license is MIT, and the only money involved is a tip jar the developer says unlocks nothing. The limits are deliberate and narrow the audience: it is iOS 18 and later only, with no Android version, and there is no Apple Watch app and no HealthKit integration. It reached 63 points on the Show HN page.

tools.name: Microsoft PowerToys (Workspaces)
tools.blurb: PowerToys is Microsoft's free bundle of Windows utilities, and Workspaces is the one that remembers a set of apps and their window positions and relaunches all of them from a desktop shortcut you can pin to the taskbar; the editor opens with Win, Ctrl, and the backtick key, any app in the layout can carry command line arguments so it starts on the file or the tabs you want, and a status dialog reports each app as launched, launching, or failed while the workspace comes up. Microsoft lists the minimum as Windows 11 or Windows 10 version 2004 on a 64-bit x64 or ARM64 processor, installable from the Microsoft Store, GitHub, WinGet, Chocolatey, or Scoop. The caveat is in Microsoft's own notes: apps set to Launch as Admin currently cannot be moved into position, and because Workspaces uses the FancyZones engine underneath it restores sizes and coordinates rather than true window snapping.

tools.name: Notesnook
tools.blurb: Notesnook is a note app with end-to-end encryption switched on by default rather than sold as an upgrade, is 100% open source under GPLv3, offers self-hostable sync, and runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and the web. Android Authority's Yash Wate put it on his September 5 list of five apps to use instead of Google Keep, for pairing that encryption with a rich text editor, media attachments, tables, notebooks, and tags. The free plan is a real plan and needs no card, but it is metered, and that is the honest caveat: 50MB of storage a month, a 10MB ceiling on any single file, 50 notebooks, 100 note versions, and 7 colors, with the Essential tier at $1.99 a month, or $19.99 a year, lifting those limits to 1GB a month.

tools.name: Simplenote
tools.blurb: Simplenote is the plainest thing on this shelf and its site is blunt about the price: the apps, backups, syncing, and sharing are all completely free, with no paid tier waiting behind them. Notes update across iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux, and the browser in real time, tags make a growing pile searchable, version history walks a note back to an earlier draft, and you can share a list with someone or publish a note to the web, with Markdown available for writing and previewing. Android Authority's Yash Wate, listing it on September 5, names the trade plainly, and it is the caveat to weigh: Simplenote carries no rich media support and no end-to-end encryption, so it suits plain text you would not mind a service provider being able to read.

tools.name: Omnisearch for Obsidian
tools.blurb: Omnisearch replaces Obsidian's built-in search with a quick switcher that ranks results by the BM25 relevance algorithm instead of listing every match, tolerates typos, honors quoted phrases, filters by file type, and can insert a link to a result straight into the note you are writing; it carries 2.1k stars, is GPL-3.0, and installs from the official Obsidian community plugins list. How-To Geek's Dibakar Ghosh named it second among five free plugins on September 5, for making a growing pile of daily notes findable again. The caveats are worth knowing before you rely on it: searching inside images, PDFs, and Office documents works only if you also add the separate Text Extractor plugin, and the project warns that its BRAT beta builds can be unstable, so take the stable release.

tools.name: Quad9
tools.kind: DNS for a device or router
tools.blurb: Quad9 is a free service that replaces the DNS resolver your ISP hands you and blocks lookups of host names known to serve malware, phishing, spyware, and botnets, using 9.9.9.9 and 149.112.112.112 (or 2620:fe::fe and 2620:fe::9 on IPv6); it is run by the not-for-profit Quad9 Foundation in Zurich, requires no sign up or account data, and states that no data containing your IP address is ever logged and that the service is GDPR compliant. Set it once in the router and every connected device behind it is covered, the site notes, including the IoT gear on the network. It reached 161 points on Hacker News on September 4 through Mullvad's September 3 announcement that it is shutting its own public encrypted DNS servers, sponsoring Quad9 instead, and telling manually configured users to migrate before November 2, 2026. The honest caveat: this is blocklist filtering of malicious host names, not antivirus, and the front page does not spell out an unfiltered option, so it is a filtered resolver by design.

tools.name: VoiceStudio
tools.blurb: VoiceStudio is an open-source, locally run alternative to ElevenLabs that the project describes as voice cloning, voice design, video dubbing, dictation, transcription, and audiobook creation across 646 languages, which in ordinary use means turning a document into audio you can listen to, or a recorded meeting into text, without an account or a per-character bill. It carries 17.8k stars, 1,345 of them gained today according to GitHub's daily trending page where it is currently listed, and it ships prebuilt installers rather than a Python checkout: a DMG for macOS 13.3 and later on Apple Silicon, an MSI for Windows 10 and 11 that does not need admin access, a Linux AppImage, and Docker images; the first launch configures its own managed Python environment. Local workflows have no subscription, API key, or usage meter. The caveats are hardware and licensing: 8GB of RAM and 10GB free disk are the stated minimum with 16GB and a 20GB SSD recommended, Intel Macs cannot run the local backend at all and need a remote one, and the default OmniVoice model is CC-BY-NC, so anything commercial means checking the model terms first.

tools.name: Breezy Weather
tools.blurb: Breezy Weather is a free Material 3 weather app for Android 5.0 and later, carrying 11.3k stars, that pulls forecasts, current observations, air quality, pollen, and severe weather alerts from more than 50 sources rather than one, and gives you 16 day forecasts with hourly data, precipitation nowcasting, detailed 24 hour charts, home screen widgets, a live wallpaper, custom icon packs, and no trackers or personal data collection; the project also lists full offline operation when Open-Meteo is the source. How-To Geek's Ismar Hrnjicevic put it first among four open-source Android apps on September 4 for having no ads or bloat while still showing conditions, forecasts, air quality, pollen, and humidity. The caveat is how you get it and how often it refreshes: the project has decided it will not publish to the Google Play Store, so you install from F-Droid, the IzzyOnDroid repository, Obtainium, or GitHub releases, and it will not do background updates more often than every 30 minutes.

tools.name: Material Files
tools.blurb: Material Files is a free GPL-3.0 file manager for Android 5.0 and later with 8.9k stars that does the jobs a stock file app usually will not: it opens, extracts, and creates archives, connects directly to FTP, SFTP, SMB, and WebDAV servers so a home NAS or a work share behaves like a local folder, handles root access, and is Linux aware about symbolic links and file permissions, with breadcrumb navigation, themes, and a night mode on top. It is built on the Java NIO2 file API and Linux system calls rather than parsing command output, which is why it is quick and does not choke on oddly named files, and it installs from Google Play, F-Droid, or a GitHub release APK. How-To Geek's Ismar Hrnjicevic, recommending it on September 4 for its Material Design 3 interface and dynamic color, names the one real gap himself: there is no recycle bin, so a delete is a delete.

tools.name: Hermit Lite Apps Browser
tools.blurb: Hermit turns a website into what Chimbori calls a Lite App, a lightweight app-like shortcut that opens the site on its own with a content blocker on by default, reader mode, dark mode, a custom icon, adjustable text size, and switches to turn images or JavaScript off alongside a data saver mode; MakeUseOf's Abhijith N Arjunan used it on September 3 to delete nine cloned apps he had been running only to hold second accounts on Amazon, Reddit, Instagram, and LinkedIn, and reports battery and RAM noticeably better afterward. The caveats are real and he says so plainly: a Lite App is a web page in a wrapper and does not feel identical to a native app, and the sandboxed profiles that make multiple simultaneous logins work sit behind Hermit's premium unlock, which is a one-time purchase rather than a subscription, alongside user scripts, tags, backup and restore, and printing.

tools.name: Tidy
tools.blurb: Tidy, from Eric Greene, is two keyboard shortcuts that work in whatever Mac app you happen to be typing in: select text and press Control Option Command T and the grammar and spelling are corrected in place, or press Control Option Command S and the same text is stripped of verbose corporate padding while the facts, the @mentions, the dates and times, and proper nouns such as brand names are left alone. Every correction runs on the model built into macOS, so nothing you select is uploaded and no API key is needed, and it is free; the caveats are the requirements, since it needs macOS 26 with Apple Intelligence switched on, which rules out older Macs, and it installs from a DMG on the developer's GitHub releases page rather than from the App Store.

tools.name: MPC-HC
tools.blurb: Media Player Classic Home Cinema is a free GPL v3 video and audio player for Windows 7 through 11, carrying 15.6k stars on the clsid2 repository, and it ships the LAV Filters codecs so H.264, HEVC, AV1, VP9, and H.266 play out of MKV, MP4, AVI, WebM, and MOV files without hunting down a codec pack, with DXVA2 and D3D11 hardware acceleration, HDR playback, frame-by-frame stepping in both directions, A-B repeat for looping a passage, adjustable playback speed, and a seekbar that previews the frame under your cursor. MakeUseOf's Tashreef Shareef, who replaced VLC with the 22MB installer on September 2, is straight about the trade: MPC-HC needs a bit of configuring to get going where VLC mostly does not, DRM-protected content will not play, and YouTube streaming works only after you wire up yt-dlp by hand.

tools.name: Files
tools.blurb: Files is a Windows file manager built with WinUI that adds what Explorer never did: browser-style tabs, a dual-pane view for dragging between two folders at once, a Mac-style column view, color-coded tags, git integration, and, How-To Geek's Ismar Hrnjicevic notes, the ability to create RAR archives, while staying close enough to Explorer's layout that there is very little to relearn. The repository carries 44.9k stars under dual MIT and MPL-2.0 licensing, and the caveat is the pricing split, because the Microsoft Store copy is a paid purchase that funds development while the classic installer from files.community and the preview build cost nothing.

tools.name: System Informer
tools.blurb: System Informer, from Winsider Seminars and Solutions, is the Task Manager that Windows 10 and later never shipped: processes are color coded by category, each one exposes its PID, command line, and resource use, real-time graphs track system activity, network connections and disk access are listed alongside, and the Find Handles or DLLs search finally answers which program is holding the file you cannot delete or rename. It is MIT licensed with 15.8k stars, runs portable with no installation, and the honest caveat is that it shows far more detail than Task Manager does, which helps only if you are willing to read it.

tools.name: CleanShot 5 with Studio Mode
tools.blurb: CleanShot is a Mac screenshot and screen recording app, and version 5 adds Studio Mode, a built-in editor that turns a raw recording into a finished video by adding zooms, trimming the mistakes, and saving the project in an editable form you can reopen later, next to the existing scrolling capture, annotation and redaction markup, on-device text recognition, and shareable cloud links. Its own pricing page puts CleanShot Basic at $35 once, covering the Mac app, a year of updates, and 1GB of cloud storage, with $19 a year afterward to keep updating; the caveats are that it needs macOS 13 or newer and that unlimited storage, a custom domain, and team management sit behind the Pro subscription at $10 per user a month billed annually.

tools.name: FUTO Keyboard
tools.blurb: FUTO Keyboard is an Android keyboard built to work with no internet connection at all, keeping swipe typing, smart autocorrect, predictive text, themes, and voice input that is transcribed on the phone instead of in a data center, and Android Police's Anu Joy lists the settings ordinary typing actually rewards: keyboard size, a number row, an arrow key row, long-press timing, whether backspace removes a character or a whole word, spacebar language switching, a personal dictionary, and blocking a word autocorrect keeps forcing on you. FUTO's documentation prices the one-time license at $6.99 through FUTO Pay or $11.99 through Google Play with no subscription, and the honest caveat is Joy's own, that Gboard stayed installed alongside it for GIF search, handwriting input, built-in translation, and the proofread and rephrase writing tools FUTO does not have.

tools.name: Ad Blocker in Firefox for iOS
tools.blurb: Mozilla's September 1 post introduces ad blocking built directly into Firefox for iOS, with no separate extension to install: it uses Apple's WebKit Content Blocker technology and the EasyList filter list to stop many third-party ads and ad-related trackers before they load, and you switch it on under Settings, then Browsing, then Ad Blocker. The caveats are worth knowing before you expect too much, because Mozilla says it is off by default, that ads served directly by the site you are visiting and ads on search results pages are not blocked, and that Firefox's own sponsored new-tab shortcuts are a separate thing it leaves alone; readers in the Hacker News thread add that the feature is arriving through a staged rollout, so the setting may not be on your phone the day you go looking for it.

tools.name: Vivaldi tab stacks on Android
tools.blurb: Vivaldi's own help pages document the feature that turns a wall of phone tabs back into a few named groups: long-press a tab and drag it onto another, or long-press and choose Add tab to new stack, and then pick how stacks appear under the Vivaldi menu, Settings, Tabs, Tab Stacking, where Two-Level Tab Stacks puts the group on a second row that shows only while one of its tabs is active, and Accordion Tabs keeps groups on the same row as ordinary tabs, expanding the one you are reading and collapsing again with a tap on the stack's name. Android Police's Marvin Velasco, who moved to it for exactly this reason on September 1, is honest that the payoff is real only if you keep a lot of tabs open, since the always-on tab bar costs screen space and the first sorting session feels cumbersome.

tools.name: Textify
tools.blurb: Textify makes the text you can see but cannot select copyable, so a cryptic error code stops being something you retype by hand: point at a Windows dialog, a system error message, a taskbar tooltip, or an old application menu, press the shortcut, which defaults to Shift plus the middle mouse button and can be reassigned to Ctrl or Alt with the left, right, or middle button, and the text opens in a selectable view with optional translation, dictionary, and web search lookups; Ramen Software's own page offers version 1.10.4 at roughly 593KB for nothing, and MakeUseOf's Sagar Naresh names the honest limit, because a window packed with a huge amount of structured text can make it choke and briefly slow whatever application you are using while it works through everything on screen.

tools.name: Orato
tools.blurb: Orato is a speaking coach that runs on an iPhone: you choose a drill such as impromptu speaking, defending a position, storytelling, or an interview, talk for a short stretch, and get back a transcript with the filler words and pauses marked, plus scores for pacing, fluency, vocabulary, and coherence, which is exactly the feedback an interview, a class, or a few minutes at a lectern rewards. Its own site says newer iPhones run the coaching on the device so the recording never leaves the phone, while older iPhones without Apple Intelligence fall back to a cloud coach; the free tier is capped at three coached sessions every seven days, and Pro is sold monthly, yearly, or as a one-time purchase, with no price published on the page to quote you.

tools.name: TeraCopy
tools.blurb: TeraCopy takes over the copy and move jobs Windows Explorer normally handles, and How-To Geek's Jorge A. Aguilar keeps it on every new PC for four reasons: a file that will not copy gets logged and skipped instead of freezing the whole queue, a second verification pass hashes what landed on disk and flags a mismatch rather than failing quietly, a transfer can be paused and later resumed from the exact byte offset where it stopped, and it hooks into drag and drop, Ctrl+C, and Ctrl+V so nothing about your habits changes; Code Sector's own page is where the limits are, since the free license covers verification, timestamps, locked files, checksum files, secure delete, and up to two copy threads, while multiple destinations, more threads, editable file lists, favorite folders, HTML and CSV reports, and commercial use belong to the $49.95 Pro license, and Aguilar is honest that if you only ever move a few small documents you do not need any of this.

tools.name: Google AI Edge Gallery
tools.blurb: Google AI Edge Gallery downloads open models onto the phone itself and runs them there with no internet connection, offering chat with a Thinking Mode that shows the reasoning steps, image analysis, audio transcription and translation, a Prompt Lab for testing, and Agent Skills that reach the calendar, reminders, maps, and phone controls such as the flashlight and volume, and it installs from Google Play, the App Store, or a direct APK in the GitHub releases for anyone without a store; the caveats are real, since XDA's Nolen Jonker found no wake word and no smart home control, the Agent Skills need the Gemma 4 models specifically, and the context window is held near 32K tokens by the RAM a phone actually has.

tools.name: Hyperfocus
tools.blurb: Hyperfocus is a planner that starts from goals rather than an inbox, walking you through flagging the few outcomes that matter, planning a weekly cycle around them, organizing the day, and then working in time-boxed focus blocks, and its own site states plainly that it is free forever with no Pro subscription, no paid plan, and no pack of AI credits to buy; the honest caveat is reach, because it is currently available only for macOS with no Windows, iPhone, or Android version, and while the planner itself is local-first and works offline, the optional AI feedback on your goals runs through third-party providers such as OpenRouter, Google, and OpenAI, free for a 14-day trial and paid directly to those providers after that.

tools.name: NEO
tools.blurb: NEO is the distraction-free word processor the novelist Hugh Howey built for his own drafting, and it asks for no account and no subscription: manuscripts save as plain files in a NEO Library folder on your own disk, chapters number and renumber themselves, one press of Enter starts a paragraph and three starts a chapter, spellcheck appears only when you call for it, and finished work exports to EPUB 3, Word, PDF, HTML, markdown, and plain text, with continuous autosave and daily zip backups kept for two weeks; the honest caveat is that it is built for writing books and nothing else, and Howey says importing existing Word, text, and markdown manuscripts is still a bit rough and might need tweaking afterward.

tools.name: Glisio
tools.blurb: Glisio records a display, a window, or a region of a Mac with system audio, microphone, and an optional webcam, then follows your cursor and clicks to generate the zoom and pan moves itself, which is how it lets you skip the heavy timeline edit, opens a built-in editor for cropping and annotating screenshots, and exports MP4 at up to 60 frames per second in widescreen, vertical, or square, all processed on the machine itself; the caveats sit on its own site, since the free tier is unlimited but stamps a watermark on every export, removing it costs $79 once for up to three Macs (listed at $47.40 through September 1) or $9.99 a month with a one-time internet check to activate, and it needs macOS 13 Ventura or later.

tools.name: SpacebarX
tools.blurb: SpacebarX is a keyboard-first outliner that keeps notes, tasks, writing, and projects inside one nested document, and its free tier carries infinite nesting, markdown, scheduling with recurring dates, cross-links, a Today view that rolls unfinished tasks forward, OPML import from other outliners, search, and templates, while the outline itself stays on your device and syncs only if you point it at your own Google Drive or Dropbox; the honest caveat is that the web app, installable as a progressive web app, is the only version available today, with the macOS, Windows, Linux, iPhone, iPad, and Android builds still listed as coming soon.

tools.name: SubSmith
tools.blurb: SubSmith is an offline-first desktop app that turns video and audio you already own into language-learning material, generating the transcript on your own machine rather than sending the media out to a transcription service, then layering on a hover dictionary, replayable lines, saved sentences that keep their audio, and one-click export to Anki flashcards across more than 99 languages; the honest caveat is that it asks you to create an account before the seven-day free trial starts, and after the trial it costs $15 a year or $40 once for a lifetime license.

tools.name: CoMaps
tools.blurb: CoMaps is a community-run fork of Organic Maps and Maps.me that searches, routes, and speaks turn-by-turn directions with no mobile data, keeps hiking trails and offline Wikipedia articles on the phone, states plainly that it does not identify you, track you, or collect information, and is free for everyone through Google Play, F-Droid, the iOS App Store, the Mac App Store, and Flathub; the caveat is coverage, since its public transit layer reaches only a growing list of cities, so check your own before you rely on it.

tools.name: Lightworks
tools.blurb: Lightworks is a long-running video editor whose free tier, listed at zero on the company's own pricing page, includes timeline editing, automatic saving, advanced transitions, and simple visual effects on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and XDA's Nolen Jonker says it replaced his Premiere Pro subscription outright, with no watermark, an installer under 100MB, proxy files for modest hardware, and background rendering while you work; the catch is stated on that same pricing page, since free exports stop at 720p and some Linux functionality is restricted.

tools.name: Simplenote
tools.kind: iOS app, also Mac, Windows, web
tools.blurb: Simplenote is Automattic's free note app, and its App Store listing shows version 4.55 holding a 4.7 average from more than 4,300 ratings while it handles notes, to-do lists, and memos in markdown with tags, pins, instant search, version history, passcode or biometric lock, widgets, and shared notes; XDA's Yash Patel counts Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and a web app in the same free tier and is straight that Simplenote carries no databases, backlinks, plugins, or knowledge-management scaffolding, and the listing itself puts the last iPhone update on November 4, 2024, so take it as a stable plain place to write rather than a system that will keep growing new features.

tools.name: Obsidian
tools.blurb: Obsidian sits at the opposite end of the shelf from Simplenote: the app itself is free with no sign-up, and XDA's Patrick Hearn stacks the MediaDB, StoryLine, Visual Notes, and Web Clipper plugins on top of it to keep an offline books-and-films log, draft a novel where Scrivener used to sit, storyboard projects on a canvas, and search fifteen years of published articles by keyword; the honest accounting is that the official pricing page charges $4 a month billed annually (or $5 monthly) for Sync across devices and $8 a month per site for Publish, an optional commercial license runs $50 a year per user, and Hearn concedes these setups do not really solve a hard problem so much as gather everything into one window.

tools.name: EasySwitch
tools.blurb: EasySwitch joins the computers on one desk so a single keyboard and mouse slide between them, the clipboard carries text, images, and files up to 10MB across, and a second machine can act as an extra display, working in any combination of macOS 13 or later, Windows 10 and 11, and Linux, with end-to-end encryption included on the free tier rather than sold as an upgrade; the limits are stated plainly on the product page, since it runs over your local network only, the free tier stops at two computers while Pro is $49 once for up to five, Linux on X11 can receive a virtual display but cannot create one, and Windows 11 wants a driver installed the first time you use the display feature.

tools.name: Todoist
tools.blurb: XDA's Chandraveer Mathur left Google Keep for Todoist because its open API and integrations let him build automations around his tasks instead of retyping them, working from projects, nested subtasks, P1 to P4 priorities, natural-language dates, and saved filters; the honest catch is the move itself, since he reports Todoist does not readily accept imports and he copied across what he needed by hand, and Todoist's own pricing page caps the free Beginner plan at 5 personal projects, 3 filter views, and one week of activity history.

tools.name: HeliBoard
tools.blurb: HeliBoard is a keyboard built on the AOSP and OpenBoard code that ships with no internet permission at all, sitting at version 4.0 on F-Droid since July 12, 2026 with about 5,900 GitHub stars, and it brings local dictionaries, themes, clipboard history, and multilingual typing; Android Police's Oluwaniyi Raji is direct that its autocorrect is less accurate than Gboard's because it does not do contextual correction, which is why he found himself reading his own sentences again, and the project itself notes that glide typing works only if you supply a closed-source library it cannot ship.

tools.name: SD Maid 2/SE
tools.blurb: SD Maid 2/SE is a GPL 3.0 Android maintenance app with roughly 7,400 GitHub stars, distributed through the Play Store, F-Droid, IzzyOnDroid, and GitHub releases, whose CorpseFinder, AppCleaner, Deduplicator, Swiper, and Media Squeeze tools go after the residual folders, caches, expansion files, and logs an ordinary file manager never shows you; Android Police's Akshay Bhalla recovered about 6GB with the paid AppCleaner, which he prices at $3 a year or $6 for a lifetime license, and he warns you to audit the list before you confirm, because a file the scanner calls junk can be a document you still want.

tools.name: uBlock Origin Lite
tools.blurb: The Manifest V3 rewrite of the best known content blocker now has 17,000,000 users and a 4.5 rating from 3,400 reviews, and it blocks ads, trackers, and miners declaratively using uBlock Origin's own filters plus EasyList, EasyPrivacy, and Peter Lowe's server list, with more rulesets available in its options; Android Authority's Andrew Grush is blunt that the lite build gives up custom filters, dynamic filtering, the element picker, and malware protection, so it suits a casual user rather than someone who tuned the original by hand.

tools.name: RustDesk
tools.blurb: RustDesk is an open-source remote desktop app with about 121,700 GitHub stars that connects out of the box through the project's relay servers, or through a server you run yourself, so you can fix a relative's computer or reach your own without a subscription; MakeUseOf's Tashreef Shareef points out that it carries no commercial-use nag screens, no session time limits, and a built-in file transfer mode, then adds the fair warning that it is not built for latency-sensitive work like gaming or video, and that the advanced server features sit behind the paid Server Pro tier.

tools.name: Tab Notes
tools.blurb: Tab Notes replaces the new tab page with a plain writing surface that handles rich text and markdown, keeps a small drawing canvas for a diagram, and exports to .txt or .md, storing everything on the machine unless you connect your own Google Drive, with no third-party servers, tracking, or ads; it is also young and small, version 2.0.2 shipped on August 16 with 491 users and a 3.8 rating from 18 reviews, so treat it as a scratchpad rather than the only copy of anything you cannot lose.

tools.name: SubtitleGenerator
tools.blurb: Drop in a video and it transcribes, flags the words it is unsure about, lets you fix text and timing, styles the captions, and exports, all in one browser tab, with your video file staying on your device and only the audio sent off for transcription; the free tier is capped at 60 minutes of subtitle time a month and 10 minutes per video, and free exports top out at 720p with a small watermark.

tools.name: debloat.dev
tools.blurb: A community directory of open-source replacements for the software that ships with hardware, sorted into ten categories including printers and scanners, peripherals, smart home, NAS and storage, and phone sync, and it keeps no tracking and no cookies unless you sign in; the listings are submitted and rated by users rather than tested by an editor, so check a project's own repository for recent activity before you install it.

tools.name: Image Toolbox
tools.blurb: Image Toolbox is one Android app for the jobs most people keep eight apps for, resizing and converting pictures, stripping EXIF data, removing backgrounds, editing PDFs, stitching images, making GIFs, generating QR codes, and building collages, free under Apache 2.0 from the Play Store, F-Droid, or GitHub with no advertisements; the honest limits are that it is Android only, wants Android 7.0 or newer, and Android Authority's Yash Wate found it needs a pass through its settings, including Launcher Mode and the output folder, before it feels productive.

tools.name: FUTO Voice Input
tools.blurb: FUTO Voice Input takes over the microphone key on an Android keyboard and does the speech recognition on the phone itself with nothing stored, free from the Play Store, F-Droid, or a roughly 70 MB download, with an optional one-time license that also covers FUTO Keyboard; How-To Geek's Bertel King is candid about the tradeoff, because you cannot speak punctuation or delete by voice, it can stop listening during a pause unless you turn on auto-stop on silence, and it garbled a product name, hearing Wispr Flow as whisper flow.

tools.name: Plane
tools.blurb: Plane is an open-source tracker for projects, work items, cycles, and roadmaps, licensed AGPL v3 with about 57,200 stars on GitHub, and its free plan costs nothing per seat for as many as 12 people, each with 500 AI credits; the caveats are the ceiling and the setup, since a thirteenth teammate moves you to the $6 per seat Pro plan, and hosting it yourself means Docker or Kubernetes rather than an installer you double-click.

tools.name: Scribus
tools.blurb: Scribus is a page layout program for the jobs Microsoft Publisher used to do, brochures, books, and business cards, with color separations, CMYK and spot colors, ICC color management, and commercial grade PDF and PostScript output, free under the GNU GPL on Windows, macOS, Linux, BSD, and ChromeOS; the caveat is the move itself, because XDA's Patrick Hearn found an interface that looks like a product of 2001 and no Microsoft Office integration, and Microsoft's own support page says 365 subscribers lose access to Publisher after October 1, 2026 and tells you to convert your files to another format first, so expect a learning curve rather than a clean import.

tools.name: Kagi Search paywall filter
tools.blurb: Kagi's changelog entry dated August 21, 2026 says the search engine added a setting for removing paywalled links from search results automatically, which spares you the click into an article you cannot finish reading; the caveat is the price, because Kagi is a subscription search engine, its free trial stops at 100 searches and 100 Assistant interactions, and the paid tiers run from Starter at $5 a month for 300 searches to Professional at $10 a month for unlimited searches and Ultimate at $25 a month.

tools.name: HyNote for Mac
tools.blurb: HyNote records system and meeting audio on the Mac itself, so no meeting bot joins your Zoom, Teams, Meet, or Webex call, and it hands back a live transcript plus a summary with key points and action items, though its own setup steps have you sign in before recording and the free plan stops a session at 120 minutes, with paid tiers starting at $6.66 a month.

tools.name: career-ops
tools.blurb: career-ops turns an AI coding CLI into a job search desk that scores a listing against your CV on a one to five rubric, tailors an ATS-ready PDF, researches the company, and tracks every application in one place, but it needs Node.js plus a separate AI CLI to run, it never submits an application for you, and its own README warns that models may hallucinate skills you do not have.

tools.name: OpenLogi
tools.blurb: OpenLogi remaps Logitech buttons, DPI, SmartShift, gestures, and lighting from your own machine with no cloud account and no telemetry, over Bolt, Unifying, Bluetooth, or a cable, though the project states plainly that it is under active development and not yet stable, and you have to quit Logitech Options+ first because only one program can own a receiver at a time.

tools.name: Grist
tools.blurb: Grist is a relational spreadsheet: columns are named and typed, records link across tables without a VLOOKUP, and charts, calendar views, and summary tables come off that same data, with forms, Python formulas, and real-time collaboration included on the free plan; the honest limit is that free hosting stops at 5,000 records per document and 10 members, so a tracker that keeps growing means either $10 per user per month or running the free open-source Community Edition on your own machine.

tools.name: NextDNS
tools.kind: Set on the router or per device
tools.blurb: Point a router or one device at NextDNS instead of the resolver your provider hands you and the logs become a live feed of every domain each device in the house tried to reach, with the device name and the timestamp, a block control beside them, and settings for where the logs live and how long they are kept, from an hour out to two years; MakeUseOf's Pankil Shah names the tradeoff without softening it, that seeing all of that traffic means trusting NextDNS with it, and the free plan covers 300,000 queries a month before it goes back to answering like ordinary non-blocking DNS.

tools.name: Flow Launcher
tools.blurb: One hotkey, Alt+Space by default, opens a single box that searches apps, files, browser bookmarks, and Windows settings, runs a calculation, fires a shell or system command, or sends the query to the web, with a plugin store to add more; the caveat is that it is Windows 10 and later only, and its file search leans on Everything or Windows Search being in place underneath it.

tools.name: GIMP
tools.blurb: GIMP is a free, open-source image editor for GNU/Linux, macOS, and Windows, currently at version 3.2.4, covering photo retouching and manipulation, original artwork, graphic design and interface elements, and scripted image work through Python and Scheme; XDA's Patrick Hearn names it on August 18 as the way out of Adobe Creative Cloud and puts the saving at $120 a year, and his honest caveat is that the interface takes real adjustment if you have been working in Photoshop, with minor feature differences remaining.

tools.name: Reckon: Decision Journal
