tools.blurb: You log a decision with the confidence you actually hold and the reasoning behind it, check in as new information arrives, then record what happened and how satisfied you were, and the app reads back the gap between the confidence you claimed and the outcomes you got, broken out by domains such as career, finances, health, and personal; it is a $1.99 one-time purchase from developer Roland Leth that keeps everything on the device and syncs only through your own iCloud with no account, and the caveats are that the listing requires iOS 26 or later, is not verified for macOS, and the calibration view does not appear until fifty decisions are logged.

tools.name: Deepmark
tools.blurb: Deepmark indexes what is inside the things you saved rather than their titles, transcribing audio in about 99 languages, describing and reading text off video frames, and summarizing pages, so a plain-language search such as the reel with the one-pan pasta trick finds the item even when those words never appear in the title, across browser bookmarks, X bookmarks, Instagram saves, and YouTube Watch Later and Liked; the caveats are real, because there is a single paid plan at $10 a month or $84 billed yearly with no free tier or trial, and adopting it means handing a third-party service your saved reading and viewing history.

tools.name: BentoPDF
tools.blurb: It is a PDF toolkit of more than 50 tools covering merging, splitting and reordering pages, annotations, forms and watermarks, conversion to and from images and Office files, plus encryption, digital signatures, and OCR, and the project's own claim is that every file is processed in your browser and never uploaded to a server; you can use the public instance the project runs at bentopdf.com or self-host it with Docker or static hosting, and XDA's Abhishek Kumar Mishra points out on August 17 that it can even be installed as a progressive web app, while the repository is honest that Office file conversion needs SharedArrayBuffer and therefore HTTPS, that digital signatures need a CORS proxy, and that some modules load from a CDN with local files as the fallback.

tools.name: Search Fixer for YouTube
tools.blurb: The extension strips the padding out of a YouTube search, hiding the For you and People also search for blocks, Shorts, playlists and mixes, and videos you have already watched, and it adds display options such as a grid view and lowercased titles; its Chrome listing reports roughly 20,000 users, a 4.5 rating from 86 reviews, and a version 10.1.2 update on August 11, 2026, and the caveat comes from How-To Geek's Ismar Hrnjicevic on August 17, who calls it barebones next to heavier alternatives, trading breadth of options for a light footprint.

tools.name: Explainpaper
tools.blurb: You upload the PDF, highlight the sentence, chart, or equation that lost you, and it hands back a plain explanation in more than 50 languages, with a chat that takes follow-up questions and links its answers back to the paper, plus automatic outlines and key points for the document as a whole; the caveat is that the free account runs on what the site calls basic AI models and leaves out full-paper summaries and saved highlights, both reserved for the $16 a month Pro tier, and How-To Geek's Jorge A. Aguilar lists it among four AI learning tools for students, pointed at complex papers and research documents.

tools.name: Chronock
tools.cost: Free plan, no card at signup
tools.blurb: It reads your real availability across Google Calendar and Microsoft Outlook, turns it into a booking page other people can pick a time on, and syncs events between separate work, personal, and project calendars so an hour taken in one shows as busy in the others; the free plan is thin on purpose, with one active booking slot, one one-way sync rule carrying busy status only, and one team member, and the site is candid that the integrated calendar view is still beta, that Microsoft Teams support and round-robin booking are planned rather than shipped, and that holiday blocking coverage varies by region.

tools.name: OCRmyPDF
tools.blurb: It slides an invisible text layer underneath the images in a scanned PDF so the file can finally be searched and its words copied, works on your own machine with nothing uploaded, reads more than 100 languages through Tesseract, and can straighten crooked pages with a deskew option and strip image noise with a clean option on the way through; the catch is stated plainly by both the project and MakeUseOf's Tashreef Shareef, that this is a command line tool with a steeper learning curve than a graphical app, that it expects Ghostscript and Tesseract installed alongside it, and that Windows users reach it through WSL, Docker, or pip rather than an installer.

tools.name: Microsoft Autoruns
tools.blurb: Microsoft's own Sysinternals utility lists every place Windows can start something automatically, well past the short list in Settings and Task Manager, taking in startup folder items, Run and RunOnce registry keys, services and drivers, scheduled tasks, and Explorer shell extensions, with a Hide Signed Microsoft Entries option to isolate what other software added and a checkbox that disables an entry rather than deleting it, and How-To Geek's Tony Phillips, who found seven Slack background processes holding 380MB of memory after startup and switched them off, is direct about the risk: not everything you find is worth disabling, so investigate an unfamiliar entry before you touch it.

tools.name: Anki
tools.blurb: A flashcard program built on spaced repetition, which its makers describe as helping you spend more time on challenging material and less on what you already know, with the free computer version available for all major platforms and AnkiDroid free on Android, and the catch stated plainly on its own page: AnkiMobile, the official iOS app, is a purchase that funds development.

tools.name: EarTrumpet
tools.blurb: It trades the single Windows volume slider for one flyout carrying a slider per running application, switches your output device from a right click, and keeps the older sound dialogs a step away, installed from the Microsoft Store or Chocolatey, and How-To Geek's Sydney Butler is straight about the limit: it adds nothing Windows cannot already do, it simply stops burying it.

tools.name: QuickLook
tools.blurb: It brings the macOS Quick Look habit to Windows, so tapping the space bar on a selected file shows a preview of images, videos, PDFs, text, code, archives, and more than a hundred formats in all, without opening the program that owns the file, and the project states both its terms and its edges plainly: free software, free forever, no ads, no tracking, no premium tiers under GPL-3.0, but the Microsoft Store build has limited Open and Save dialog support, so the installer from its GitHub releases page is the fuller one.

tools.name: ShareX
tools.blurb: One free utility that covers screenshots, annotation, screen recording, OCR, and quick editing under keyboard shortcuts you assign yourself, capturing the whole screen, a single window, or a custom region without opening a bulky interface first, and its own site keeps the terms to four claims, free forever, open source, no account required, no advertisements, after more than eighteen years of development, while the limit sits in that same description: it is a screenshot tool for Windows, so a Mac or a phone gets nothing from it.

tools.name: FluidVoice
tools.blurb: Dictation that runs on the machine itself, with a live transcription preview while you speak, a command mode for driving the Mac by voice, and an optional local model the project calls Fluid Intelligence for formatting and capitalization, free under GPLv3 and installed by Homebrew or a release download, and the requirements are the honest catch: macOS 15 Sequoia or later, Apple silicon for most models with Intel Macs falling back to Whisper, microphone and accessibility permissions, about 1 GB of disk for the voice model and roughly 3.5 GB more if you add the enhancement one, and no Windows or iOS build exists yet.

tools.name: SpotAngels
tools.blurb: A parking app that maps free against paid street parking, sends a reminder before street cleaning or another rule turns your space into a ticket, and collects garage deals, which is the kind of thing that pays for itself the first time it works, and its limit is geography rather than price: the free tier is real with a paid SpotAngels Plus sitting on top of it, but the map is built city by city, and the company's own site names ten, New York, San Francisco, Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, Boston, Washington DC, San Diego, Toronto, and Montreal, before pointing to more.

tools.name: Arena.ai
tools.blurb: One browser page that gathers a range of proprietary and open AI models and runs two of them side by side on the same prompt, so you can see which one actually answers your question before paying for any of them, and the catch is printed on the site itself: your conversations are disclosed to the AI providers and may be shared publicly to support AI research, which is why it warns you not to submit personal or sensitive information, while Oluwaseun Bamisile found the free allowance differs sharply by model, roughly five messages on one newer model against about twenty on another before a limit that resets in about an hour, with image and video generation capped at two a day.

tools.name: Quetta
tools.blurb: A Chromium based browser that blocks ads and trackers by default, installs extensions from the Chrome Web Store and Edge Add-ons on a phone rather than only on a desktop, and saves supported MP4, WebM, and HLS video for offline playback, with reader mode, page translation, and fingerprint protection sitting alongside, and Oluwademilade Afolabi names the two costs plainly: the code is proprietary, so nobody outside the company can audit it the way Firefox can be audited, and the Android build runs on Chromium 148.0.7778.217, a version the company's own release notes date to August 4, which means security patches can reach you later than they reach Chrome.

tools.name: KidScreen
tools.blurb: It gives a child a fixed shelf of YouTube videos a parent has added by hand, with no search box, no recommendations, and no endless scroll, and the makers say plainly that it is free because they are building it so families stay in control, which is also where its limits live: it needs a family account before anyone watches anything, every video on the shelf is one you put there yourself, so the shelf stays interesting only while you keep feeding it, and the site names no supported devices, so treat it as a browser page rather than a television app until it says otherwise. It drew 33 points and 28 comments on Hacker News today.

tools.name: Rowboat
tools.blurb: An AI workspace that keeps its memory on your own disk, indexing email, meetings, and notes into a linked knowledge graph written as plain Markdown files and sitting beside a built-in mail client, notes, browser, and meeting transcription, with downloadable builds for Mac, Windows, and Linux and no Docker to set up, and the honest catch is that it brings no brain of its own: you point it at a local model through Ollama or LM Studio or supply your own paid provider key, and the parts that make it useful, Gmail and Calendar through Google sign-in, voice, and web search, each want their own connection before they work, which MakeUseOf's Mahnoor Faisal also found took setup past the install.

tools.name: Hyperspace
tools.blurb: It finds files whose contents are identical and hands back the space the copies waste without removing any of them, using a standard macOS file system feature to replace them with space-saving clones, and both the catch and the argument are about money: the scan is free and shows you the savings first, but reclaiming them is the paid part, at $9.99 for a month, $19.99 for a year, or $49.99 for a lifetime unlock from Hypercritical LLC, which is precisely what the Hacker News thread of 85 points and 62 comments spent the night disputing, some calling the unpriced scan a dark pattern and others calling it ordinary shareware.

tools.name: Write.md
tools.blurb: A writing app that leaves your work as ordinary Markdown files on your own disk with no account and no telemetry, installed from a .dmg on its releases page, and it spends its effort on how the page feels, with appearance profiles covering typography, color, opacity, glass effects, backgrounds, and window borders, optional Vim keys, and spelling and style help that runs on the machine instead of in a cloud service, though the maker is equally plain about the limits: it runs on Apple silicon Macs only, ships no bundled themes so each profile starts from nothing, corrects basic US English and no other language, and syncs to nothing at all, which is the point until the day you want the same draft on a second device.

tools.name: Craft
tools.blurb: A block-based editor for notes, tasks, and documents that lets you drag whole sections into a new order, nest subpages under a project, and keep daily notes, tasks, and a calendar in one place, and the free plan draws its lines clearly: 1,500 blocks, 1 GB of storage, 25 MB per upload, seven days of version history, and 15 AI credits, while XDA's Parth Shah grants it is not a complete replacement for Word on complex formatting, academic references, or heavily structured corporate documents.

tools.name: Rembg
tools.blurb: Cuts the background out of a photo and writes a transparent PNG, working on a single file, a whole folder, or a folder it watches, with more than fifteen models to choose from and a local server mode if you want one, and the catches are real: it installs through pip and wants Python 3.11 to 3.13, and How-To Geek's Nick Lewis warns that the lighter models struggle with fine detail like hair, that repairing a bad edge means opening GIMP or Krita, and that some downloadable model weights carry non-commercial licenses even though the software itself is free.

tools.name: Buildin.AI
tools.blurb: A Notion-style workspace that treats a mind map as a native page type beside its pages and folders, and XDA's Nolen Jonker reports it also carries a timeline view and lets you choose GPT, Gemini, or DeepSeek as the model behind its writing and its questions about your own notes, with the free plan capped hard at 2 GB of storage, 5 MB per file, 300 mind-map nodes, and ten AI chat requests a month before the $10 add-on that raises it to 3,000.

tools.name: AndroMeld
tools.kind: Mac app for an Android phone
tools.blurb: It runs your Android apps in their own resizable Mac windows and handles phone files in Finder while syncing notifications and the clipboard over USB or Wi-Fi, with the honest catch that it needs macOS 15 or later and the free tier is capped by a weekly allowance that resets on its own.

tools.name: Kaneo
tools.blurb: Kaneo is an open-source project tracker with board and list views, owners, due dates, priorities, and GitHub issue sync, free forever under the MIT license when you self-host it, though the free path means running it yourself with Docker because the hosted Cloud Personal plan is $40 a year after a 14-day trial.

tools.name: Glyphi: Speed Reader
tools.blurb: Flashes an imported book, PDF, article, or web page one word at a time so your eyes stay still, keeps your place across Apple devices through iCloud, and builds its summaries on the device itself, and the App Store listing is plain about the limits: the free tier stops at five saved readings, 550 words a minute, and the Endurance training mode, unlimited imports and speeds up to 1,200 words a minute cost $4.99 a month or $39.99 a year, and the listing warns that AI generated results may occasionally contain errors.

tools.name: Legacy Notepad
tools.blurb: Rebuilds the plain Windows Notepad in C++17 and the Win32 API with word wrap, font choice, zoom, find and replace, printing, an always-on-top window, and UTF-8, UTF-16, and ANSI encodings, and no AI anywhere, which is the whole point of it, and the project names its own trade-offs: it is a young, maintainer-led effort rather than an application tested at Microsoft's scale, its background image modes shift with DPI scaling, and Windows Defender has flagged an x86 build.

tools.name: Zen Browser
tools.blurb: A Firefox-based browser built on Firefox 153.0.3 that aims squarely at productivity, moving tabs into a vertical sidebar where long titles are actually readable and adding split view for two pages side by side, Glance previews for links, pinned tabs, and customizable layouts, and the XDA write-up that put it back in front of readers supplies the honest caveat: no single feature here is revolutionary, and Firefox has offered vertical tabs for a while now.

tools.name: Wispr Flow Notetaker
tools.blurb: Captures a meeting locally through your Mac rather than joining the call as a visible bot, then names the speakers and returns a summary organized around decisions and next steps that you can search later, and its own page states the limits: Mac only with Windows listed as coming soon, English only for now, and free-plan use that becomes unlimited on Flow Pro, which the same site's plans page prices at $15 a user each month, or $12 billed yearly.

tools.name: Wondering, learn anything
tools.kind: iPhone, iPad, M1 Mac or later
tools.blurb: Turns a subject you have been meaning to learn into a course of short lessons, podcasts, and exercises pitched at what you already know, with the App Store listing naming the limits: it is English only, it wants iOS 14 or later or a Mac with an M1 chip, and unlimited daily lessons plus up to 15 new courses a month sit behind Pro at $14.99 a month or $107.99 a year.

tools.name: Screen Awesome
tools.blurb: Records a tab, a screen, or your camera to MP4 from inside Chrome, glides a zoom to every click, and leaves the arrows, blur, redaction, and step numbers unlocked with no watermark and no sign-in, and the honest catch is where the files live: recordings stay in the browser's own storage on the machine that made them, and removing the extension deletes them with it.

tools.name: Wispr Flow Notetaker
tools.kind: Notetaker on Mac only for now
tools.blurb: Listens to a meeting through your Mac's own audio instead of joining the call, then hands back a cleaned transcript, a summary, and action items you can search later, and the plan page is plain about the limits: the notetaker runs on Mac only for now with other platforms listed as coming soon, and unlimited dictation plus more meetings kept for longer costs $15 a user each month, or $12 billed yearly.

tools.name: Pandoc
tools.blurb: Turns one document into another from a single command, and John MacFarlane's twentieth anniversary post counts 51 input formats and 76 output formats, so a Markdown draft can leave as a Word file, an EPUB, or a slide deck; the honest catch is that PDF output still leans on a LaTeX engine you install separately, MiKTeX on Windows, BasicTeX or TinyTeX on macOS, TeX Live on Linux.

tools.name: space ocr
tools.blurb: Reads photographed receipts, statements, and forms into a table where every value shows where on the page it came from, and marks the readings it is unsure of as needs_review instead of guessing quietly, with the limits stated plainly on its pricing page: the free tier is 100 pages a month across three sheets, and exporting a CSV spends one of those pages.

tools.name: Voicebox
tools.blurb: Keeps speech work on your own machine, with push-to-talk dictation into any app, speech generation across 23 languages and seven engines, and voice cloning from samples you supply, and the project states its own limits plainly: there are no prebuilt Linux binaries yet, and automatic pasting after dictation is still not implemented on Windows or Linux.

tools.name: Finamie
tools.blurb: Logs a purchase when you hold a button and say it out loud, pulling the amount, currency, category and details out of your own voice in English or Spanish, with the caveat that the free plan stops at 30 voice transactions a month and one default analytics widget, and everything past that is $39.99 a year.

tools.name: ssh.place
tools.blurb: Type ssh ssh.place and you are standing on a shared canvas of 200 by 60 cells where anyone can place a colored block, which is the charm and also the caveat: the wait is 15 seconds per block and survives a reconnect, text is rejected outright, and the canvas is wider than most terminal windows, so you scroll to see all of it.

tools.name: Isopolis
tools.blurb: Draws San Francisco, and only San Francisco, as an isometric pixel city over an OpenStreetMap and CARTO base with neighborhood data from DataSF, and the honest caveat comes from its maker, who says the style was generated by a model he trained and that it still turns some roads into water and invents structures that are not there.

tools.name: Dark Hours
tools.blurb: Rates a location's sky on the Bortle scale and lays out the night around it, giving sunset, the astronomical night window, sunrise, moon phase and the darkest direction to face, but it models light pollution from population data rather than satellite radiance and states its own bias plainly: within about 15 km of a mid-size city it reads about one Bortle class too dark, so assume the real sky is worse.

tools.name: bitchat
tools.blurb: Carries messages phone to phone over a Bluetooth mesh with no accounts, phone numbers or central servers, and uses the Nostr protocol when there is internet, though the project warns that only App Store builds or source you verified yourself can be trusted, and its whitepaper notes the mesh carries a persistent per-device identifier that a nearby radio can observe.

tools.name: Zen Whisper
tools.blurb: Types dictation into any Mac app from a keyboard shortcut with recognition running on the machine instead of in the cloud, free for 3,000 words a week once the 14-day trial ends, and its makers concede that on-device models handle technical jargon poorly, which they answer with a custom dictionary and snippets rather than a larger model.

tools.name: Meshdiff
tools.blurb: Takes two STL, 3MF or OBJ files and renders a voxel diff in the browser, green for added material and red for removed, with tolerance adjustable from 0.05 to 1mm and volume delta metrics; its author says nothing is uploaded to any server, and one commenter reported that multi-group OBJ files show only the first group.

tools.name: Invidious
tools.blurb: Opens YouTube through a public instance with no ads, no tracking and no JavaScript required, though the project says plainly that it does not use YouTube's official APIs and takes no responsibility for the third-party instances it lists.

tools.name: G'MIC 4.0
tools.blurb: Brings the filter count to 644 with six new ones in this release, among them Pixel Stretch and Heightfield Warp, but it is a plugin rather than an app: you run it inside GIMP, Krita, Photoshop or Affinity Photo, from the command line, or in a browser at G'MIC Online.

tools.name: Elevators, an interactive explainer
tools.blurb: Lets you set building height, car count and passenger flow, then watch LOOK, destination dispatch and other algorithms rearrange the wait-time histogram, which is the whole of it: this is a browser essay with simulators inside, not an app you keep.

tools.name: Yamanote 3D
tools.blurb: Puts you inside an E235 carriage on Tokyo's Yamanote loop, where you walk the car, sit down, listen to the station announcements and step off at a stop, with nothing to win or finish: its maker pitches it as calm background for studying or working.

tools.name: EssayKraft
tools.blurb: A paginated writing app with automatic citations, built-in reference lookup and DOCX export, bought once with no subscription and no account, though the App Store listing asks for macOS 26 or iPadOS 26, which rules out older machines.

tools.name: Gander
tools.blurb: Opens PDFs, Word and Excel files, images, video, audio, Markdown and code entirely offline without asking for storage permission, though you sideload the APK from GitHub because it is not on the Play Store or F-Droid.

tools.name: mectrics
tools.blurb: Folds CPU, memory, battery, network, disk, GPU and fan readings into a single menu bar item that stays quiet until a threshold holds, and its own launch notes concede it goes less deep than paid rivals such as iStat Menus.

tools.name: Focus Room
tools.blurb: Put focusroom.club/ in front of any YouTube URL and the video reopens as a distraction-free course with transcript search and timestamped notes, though launch-day testers hit YouTube quota errors and the notes cannot be exported yet.

tools.name: Kaneo
tools.blurb: Runs kanban boards and issue tracking on a machine you own from a Docker Compose file, and its makers state the trade-off plainly: a deliberately minimal design with fewer features than Jira or Linear.

tools.name: SoundGate Guitar
tools.blurb: It listens through the microphone and draws what you are playing on a live fretboard, with an AI tutor that answers questions and builds practice routines, plus a tuner and metronome; it is an Apple-only app, so Android players are out of luck.

tools.name: Yap, on-device dictation for macOS
tools.blurb: Press a shortcut, talk, press it again, and your words appear in whatever text field you were in, using Apple's built-in speech APIs with no model to download and no network calls; it needs macOS 26 or later on Apple Silicon, and Intel Macs are deliberately not supported.

tools.name: CheapFoodMap
tools.blurb: A map of meals under $10 across a dozen featured cities including New York, Chicago, Houston and Los Angeles, with a price-verified date shown on each spot; the entries are crowdsourced, so coverage thins out fast once you pan away from the big cities.

tools.name: tale.fyi
tools.blurb: One link opens a whole book, keeps your place on the device, and lets you swap between reading and listening; an account is optional and only syncs progress, but the library is public domain material from Project Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks and LibriVox, so nothing modern is on the shelf.

tools.name: TokenTown
tools.blurb: Type a prompt and watch a single token travel through an isometric city where each district is one stage of a language model, from tokenizing to attention to sampling; the model is deliberately tiny and its weights are random and untrained, so the words it produces are noise and only the machinery is real.

workflows.title: Five Excel tools for cleaning up the spreadsheet somebody else built, starting with Go To Special
workflows.dek: Audit first, then fix How-To Geek's Tony Phillips opens Find and Select and runs Go To Special to catch every blank cell before touching anything, marks duplicates and inconsistencies through Highlight Cells Rules in conditional formatting so the underlying data stays as it was, breaks crammed cells apart with TEXTSPLIT on a comma, a pipe or a space and pastes the result as values before deleting the source, and saves Excel tables and named ranges built through Create from Selection for last, once the sheet is clean enough to deserve them.

workflows.title: Audit the accounts still tied to your old phone number before a stranger is handed it
workflows.dek: Search, then re-point How-To Geek's Arol Wright notes that a cancelled US number usually re-enters the reuse pool within 45 to 90 days, and that Princeton researchers found 100 of 259 recycled numbers already tied to credentials leaked online, leaving a new holder needing only the texted code; his audit searches your email for phrases like verification code, works down from the carrier, email, Apple or Google account, bank and payment services, swaps the number out for an authenticator app, a passkey or a hardware key, changes it inside messaging apps using their own change-number tools before the line goes dark, checks the secondary services from pharmacies to airlines to delivery apps, and deletes the dormant accounts instead of updating them.
needs: An email account you can search
A password manager or account list

workflows.title: Switch off the Windows animations and a four-year-old laptop stops feeling four years old
workflows.dek: Three switches, one menu MakeUseOf's Pankil Shah turns off Animation effects and Transparency effects under Settings, Accessibility, Visual effects, then searches for adjust the appearance and performance of Windows and picks Adjust for best performance, or takes the Custom option to keep Smooth edges of screen fonts and Show thumbnails instead of icons, and pairs it with Best performance under Settings, System, Power and battery; he is honest about the trade, that the interface looks a bit weird at first, that the gain lands on older or budget machines rather than new high-end ones, that the power mode costs a laptop battery life, and that the hidden Ultimate Performance plan is not worth its heat.

workflows.title: Three settings worth changing on the Firefox page everybody is warned away from
workflows.dek: Three names, three values MakeUseOf's Afam Onyimadu sets browser.urlbar.trimURLs to false so the address bar shows the whole address, which makes a redirect or a local page easy to read and compare, sets browser.tabs.closeWindowWithLastTab to false so closing the final tab leaves the window standing, and sets browser.urlbar.decodeURLsOnCopy to true so a copied link arrives readable rather than percent-encoded; he prints the trade in each case, that the first is purely visual and changes nothing about security, that the second costs you a quick way to quit if you used it deliberately, and that some services still expect the encoded form.

workflows.title: Four standing orders for ChatGPT: a nightly news brief, a morning calendar read, a price watch, and a refocus nudge
workflows.dek: Write the prompt once MakeUseOf's Judy Sanhz schedules a 7:30 PM task for the five biggest tech stories of the last 24 hours, naming the topics, the lookback window, the count and what to leave out, an 8 AM task that reads Google Calendar back with the overlaps, the back to back meetings and the free blocks, a daily price check on an Amazon tripod told to stay silent unless it hits $17 or less, and a five minute nudge to end a break on time; tasks can be edited or run by hand at any point, but nothing arrives unless notifications are on in the Tasks section, and the plan sets the ceiling at three tasks on Free and Go, five on Plus, ten on Business and Edu and fifteen on Pro and Enterprise.
needs: A ChatGPT account (3 tasks on free)
Notifications on in the Tasks section
Google Calendar linked for the briefing

workflows.title: Five Chrome features that end the tab hoard: groups, vertical tabs, reading mode, split view, and Ask Gemini
workflows.dek: Group first, then split Android Police's Anu Joy stops treating open tabs as a to-do list by right-clicking a tab and choosing Add tab to new group so related pages travel together, right-clicking the tab strip and picking Show tabs vertically to read full titles down the side, right-clicking a page and opening it in reading mode, which strips the clutter and offers read aloud at an adjustable speed, and right-clicking a tab or a link to open it in a split view so two pages sit side by side during research; the fifth is Ask Gemini, which takes the current tab as context so there is no need to explain what is on the screen, and the standing limit is availability, since not every feature works on every page or platform.
needs: Ten minutes to sort what is open
A Google account for Ask Gemini

workflows.title: Turn a flat task list into a self-updating Excel tracker with checkboxes, three counters and a progress bar
workflows.dek: Table first, formulas second How-To Geek's Tony Phillips types the tasks and a Status column, presses Ctrl+T to make it a table, renames the table T_Tasks in the Table Design tab, and drops a checkbox into every Status cell from the Insert tab, after which the arithmetic writes itself: COUNTIFS on TRUE over ROWS of the table gives the percentage complete, COUNTIFS on FALSE counts what is pending, COUNTIFS on TRUE counts what is done; conditional formatting on the rule that the status cell equals TRUE greys out and strikes through a finished task, a data bar scaled from 0 to 1 turns the percentage into a bar, and switching off gridlines makes the sheet stop looking like a spreadsheet; the requirement to check before starting is the checkbox itself, which needs Excel for Microsoft 365 or Excel for the web.
needs: Excel for Microsoft 365 or the web
A task list you already keep

workflows.title: Seven Google Maps settings worth fixing before the next long drive, starting with the offline map
workflows.dek: Download the map first Android Police's Jade Bryan Jardinico, writing after a 400 mile drive, starts by downloading the route's area under the profile icon and Offline maps, switches on the traffic layer in Android Auto route options for the green, orange and red read of the road ahead, enters the car and fuel type under Your vehicles so routing accounts for efficiency and charging ports, and turns on driving notifications and Bluetooth beacons under Navigation settings so an ETA appears when the car connects and tunnels stop scrambling the position; voice guidance gets softened under Sound and voice rather than muted, a Gemini shortcut is built from Customize launcher for hands-free requests, and the limit that matters most is stated plainly, that an offline map carries no live traffic, hazards or incident updates.
needs: Wi-Fi to download the offline map
Android Auto for the in-car settings

workflows.title: Six small automations, each worth two minutes, from meeting notes that file themselves to a shopping list that waits at the store
workflows.dek: One trigger, one rule XDA's Anurag Singh lets Notion AI Meeting Notes turn the action items it hears into task entries, hands the Downloads folder to Sortly so each file is renamed by date, source and type and moved where it belongs, keeps renewal and expiry dates in a Notion database that raises a reminder 30 days and then 7 days out, maps a short trigger such as ;email onto the full text in the keyboard's own expansion settings, pins the shopping list to the store's location in the iPhone Reminders app, and gives midnight and 7 a.m. appliance switching to a smart plug's companion app, all on his one rule: a task with a clear trigger that always ends the same way is worth a few minutes of setup.
needs: A smart plug for the last one

workflows.title: Read the three-minute voice message instead of playing it, after one switch in Google Messages
workflows.dek: One setting, then a button Android Police's Ben Khalesi opens Google Messages, taps the profile picture, goes to Messages settings and Voice message transcription and switches it on, after which every arriving voice note carries a View transcript button above the recording; he pairs it with two honest limits, that a message recorded in a windstorm or a loud bar will defeat the transcription and that plain text strips the tone carrying sarcasm or disappointment, so he keeps his own voice notes under 90 seconds and asks senders to type out the addresses and dates.

workflows.title: Three free settings on a Galaxy phone that stop spam calls before it rings
workflows.dek: Three toggles, no subscription How-To Geek's Tyler Dupont opens the Phone app, taps the three dot menu and Settings, and switches on Caller ID and Spam Protection, which checks Hiya's database and can block everything flagged as spam or only the high risk numbers, then turns on call screening, where Galaxy AI answers first, asks who is calling and transcribes the reply live for either suspected spam or every unknown number, and holds Block numbers in reserve to refuse anyone not in contacts, the nuclear option that also turns away legitimate calls from businesses; all three are free, though the AI screening needs a newer Galaxy.
needs: Five minutes in the Phone app

workflows.title: Five Android automations you can build tonight without code, from a phone that silences itself to a saved parking spot
workflows.dek: Rules first, app second How-To Geek's Joe Fedewa starts with what the phone already does, an alert mode that changes itself on a Wi-Fi network or at a location, under Settings, System, Rules on a Pixel or in Modes and Routines on a Samsung Galaxy, then NFC tags for study, sleep, and driving modes, and a Galaxy rule under Settings, Connections, Wi-Fi, Intelligent Wi-Fi that drops Wi-Fi when you leave home; the last two run on MacroDroid, a text to one person when you leave work and the one he calls the most involved of the set, a parking note triggered by the car Bluetooth disconnecting that saves the GPS spot and opens it in Google Maps, and the limitation he states plainly is that Samsung leads here, leaving Pixel owners on third-party apps and unable to use NFC tags with the built-in Rules at all.

workflows.title: Rebuild the daily planner, the Trello board, and the whiteboard inside one Obsidian vault
workflows.dek: Four plugins, one vault XDA's Parth Shah spent a month folding separate apps back into Obsidian's own parts, using Daily Notes with the Calendar plugin in place of a planner, the Kanban plugin for Trello-style boards of columns and cards, Canvas for mapping ideas out visually, and Beautitab for a start page with a search bar that he says almost makes the vault feel like his own private search engine, all dressed in the Encore theme; two limits belong on the label, that he still sends team projects to proper collaboration tools and keeps this setup for personal work, and that he is openly uneasy about Beautitab, a plugin that has not been updated in two years.

workflows.title: Work the Google Keep notes screen like an inbox: label it, archive it, and let search do the finding
workflows.dek: Label, then archive XDA's Mahnoor Faisal treats the main Notes screen as an inbox, adding the relevant label to each note and archiving it so it leaves the view without leaving the search, and leans on a search that filters by type, label, and color and by categories Keep recognizes on its own, including books, music, travel, places, TV, and food, and that reads text inside images too; the rest is plumbing already sitting there, since Copy to Google Docs turns a note into a document and Keep opens in the Docs sidebar to drag notes from, Keep reminders feed into Google Tasks and surface on Calendar, and a voice note is saved with its transcription; the one piece to wait for is Keep Live, the feature meant to structure messy thoughts, which she says she does not have access to yet.
needs: Google Keep on phone or web
Ten minutes to name your labels

workflows.title: Windows 11 may be throttling your PC on purpose, and two settings put the speed back
workflows.dek: Two toggles, two minutes How-To Geek's Goran Damnjanovic points at Energy Saver, which Windows 11 can leave switched on permanently, and at the Best power efficiency power mode, a pair that together hold CPU clock speeds down, slow app launches, weaken gaming performance, and can drop the display to 60Hz even with the machine plugged in; the fix is to turn the Energy Saver tile off in Quick Settings, or clear Always use energy saver under System, Power and battery, Energy saver, then set Power mode to Best performance on mains and Balanced on battery; the tradeoff is real and worth keeping in view, because those same settings are what buy you quieter fans, less heat, and a longer afternoon away from the charger.
needs: Quick Settings in the system tray

workflows.title: Stop using the inbox as a to-do list: send each email to Google Tasks or Calendar the moment you read it
workflows.dek: Two buckets, one rule Android Police's Anu Joy opens an actionable message, uses the three dot menu, and either picks Add to Tasks, which keeps a link back to the email and drops it into the Tasks side panel beside Calendar, or picks Create event, which builds a calendar entry from the subject and body; the rule that makes it hold is a single sentence, if you need to check it off it goes in Tasks and if you need to plan your day around it it goes on the Calendar, and the one snag to watch is that a new event quietly carries the other people on the thread as invitees, so remove them when the reminder is only for you.
needs: One sorting rule you will keep

workflows.title: Give the browser one workspace per part of your life and most desktop apps stop earning their space
workflows.dek: Pin it, do not install it XDA's Mahnoor Faisal built four workspaces in Zen Browser, one each for writing, work, college, and personal, then pinned the tools she opens every day, Spotify, Google Docs, Notion, Slack, ChatGPT, Claude, Gmail, Google Calendar, Todoist, and Adobe Express, so the pinned row behaves like a dock and split view puts two of them side by side; her point is that Spotify, Slack, Adobe Express, Notion, Asana, Outlook, Zoom, and the AI chatbots all have capable web versions, and Chrome users can approximate the same thing with tab groups, but she is careful not to oversell it, keeping real desktop apps for development work in VS Code and for features that do not translate to a browser tab.
needs: A browser with workspaces or tab groups
The web versions of your apps
An hour to sort the tabs

workflows.title: Seven Windows 11 features worth switching off tonight, from OneDrive syncing to Bing results in Start
workflows.dek: Mostly just Settings How-To Geek's Zachary Boddy unlinks OneDrive under File Explorer, OneDrive, Settings, Account, Unlink this PC, uninstalls Copilot from Installed apps and reassigns its keyboard key under Bluetooth and devices, Keyboard, stops the Widgets board opening on hover and switches its news feed off, strips Recent, suggestions, the mobile device row, and account notifications out of Personalization, Start, turns off Phone Link and cross device access, removes Xbox, Xbox Live, and Game Mode, and blocks Bing web results in search; the caveats are stated where they matter, since unlinking OneDrive leaves your local files exactly where they are, while the last steps, removing Phone Link and the Game Bar outright and disabling Bing results, need PowerShell, administrator rights, and a restart.

workflows.title: The Windows 11 tweaks everyone recommends, tested: most of them cost more than they give back
workflows.dek: Four myths, one rule XDA's Abhishek Kumar Mishra worked through four optimizations people repeat constantly and found most of them are a tax on the experience: switching animations and visual effects off buys nothing on a machine modern enough to run the OS at all, third party cleaners and registry optimizers he describes as adware disguised as the fix, with Microsoft itself discouraging them and the built in Disk Cleanup doing the honest version of the job, disabling services wholesale is the risky one, since Xbox and telemetry are safe to stop but Windows Update and the firewall are not, and turning hibernation off is backwards, because it helps recovery and Fast Startup is the setting actually worth disabling; his verdict is qualitative rather than benchmarked, so read it as a caution against micromanaging Windows rather than as measured numbers.
needs: The tweak list someone handed you

workflows.title: Your USB stick is not dying yet: back it up, reformat it, and copy the files back in one pass
workflows.dek: Erase before write How-To Geek's Sydney Butler explains why a cheap flash drive loses write speed the longer you own it, since flash cannot overwrite in place and the whole block holding the data has to be erased before anything new lands, and a budget drive has none of the controller sophistication an SSD uses for garbage collection, which is why the slowdown hits smaller drives sooner and shows up in writes while reads stay unaffected; the fix is unglamorous and works, copy everything off, reformat the drive, preferably to exFAT, and copy the files back in a single operation so the controller gets the chance to cut fragmentation and rebuild free blocks, and he is straight about the ceiling, because flash memory does wear out eventually and a replacement drive is the real answer.
needs: The USB drive that got slow

workflows.title: Write the draft yourself, let an LLM find the flaws, then fix every one of them in your own words
workflows.dek: Editor, not ghostwriter The sockpuppet.org post keeps the first draft entirely human, feeds it to a model only so problems get flagged, then rewrites each flagged passage by hand and asks a fresh session which version reads better, under two rules that do the real work: you may not use a single word an LLM suggests to you, and you ignore its encouragement, because a model praises everything and the rethinking it talks you out of is where your own voice comes from; the piece is honest that the reliable help is mechanical, overused passive voice, repeated phrases, filler words, and paragraphs sitting in the wrong place, and it needs no special software, since an ordinary chat window runs the whole loop.
needs: Any chat LLM you already use
A second fresh session to compare

workflows.title: Put the phone on the table and let Google Meet write up the meeting everyone is already sitting in
workflows.dek: Take notes for me Android Police opens the Meet app for a meeting where everyone is already in the room, taps Take notes and then Start taking notes, sets the phone face up on the table, and stops it at the end, and Gemini returns a summary, an action item list, and a full transcript as a Google Doc filed in Drive with the link emailed over; the limits are stated up front, since the feature reached Android on August 11, 2026 with iOS and the web following, it wants a meeting of at least fifteen minutes and one language throughout, it can be paused when something sensitive comes up, and it needs an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra plan or a supported Workspace subscription rather than a free account.
needs: Google AI Pro, Ultra, or Workspace plan
Everyone in the room told first

workflows.title: Resize the Gboard keyboard before blaming autocorrect, because most of the typos are mis-taps
workflows.dek: Millimeters, not machine learning Android Police's Ali Salman Zia traced his typos to thumbs landing a few millimeters off target rather than to autocorrect failing, so he opened the four square toolbar icon in Gboard, used Resize to raise the keyboard height and widen the gap between the rows, then cleared the stale entries under Settings and Dictionary and added the names he keeps mistyping, turned auto-correction down under Corrections and suggestions while leaving the suggestion strip on, and switched the number row on for entering digits; the honest part is the adjustment period, because the thumbs have to learn the new geometry before the error rate falls.

workflows.title: Switch off the 1999 compatibility mode on the 2.4GHz band and every device in the house gets airtime back
workflows.dek: One shared channel MakeUseOf's Jonathon Jachura explains that 802.11b support, still on by default on most routers, makes the radio send beacons thousands of times an hour at the slowest speed that old standard allows, and since only one radio transmits at a moment on a shared channel, everyone else waits; on UniFi he walks Settings, WiFi, the network's advanced section, 2.4 GHz Data Rate Control, and slides the minimum from 1Mbps to 12Mbps, while on TP-Link, Netgear, and Asus he switches the 2.4GHz Mode from 802.11b/g/n mixed to 802.11g/n or 802.11n/ax only, and the tradeoff is said plainly: it cuts off any true 802.11b device, which in most homes means nothing made after about 2005, though 6Mbps is the softer setting and gear at the fringe of coverage can drop out sooner.
needs: A list of your oldest devices

workflows.title: Four built-in Windows tools that repair the PC on a schedule: Task Scheduler, DISM, SFC, and Quick Machine Recovery
workflows.dek: Scheduled, not reactive How-To Geek's Arol Wright repairs the component store with DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, restores protected system files from it with sfc /scannow, and wires the pair into Task Scheduler with highest privileges, the SYSTEM account, and a Conditions rule that keeps the scans on mains power, leaving Quick Machine Recovery under Settings, System, Recovery for the boot failures, with the limits said out loud: SFC needs DISM to have run first, a repair can take from several minutes to much longer, and Quick Machine Recovery is built for widespread outages and needs a network connection to reach its fix.

workflows.title: Five Excel annoyances with five-minute fixes, from Ctrl+Z reaching into another workbook to arrow keys inserting cell references
workflows.dek: Five settings, one sitting How-To Geek's Tony Phillips opens unrelated files in separate Excel instances by holding Alt and right-clicking the icon so one undo cannot reach into another workbook, teaches the fill handle the alphabet by adding A to Z under File, Options, Advanced, Edit Custom Lists, unchecks Allow editing directly in cells so a long formula stops covering the cells you are trying to select, opens a second window on the same workbook from View, New Window so Alt+Tab moves between worksheets, and presses F2 when the arrow keys start inserting cell references instead of moving the cursor.

workflows.title: Rebuild the Quick Settings panel: shrink the tiles for their long-press actions, cut the dead ones, add a free tile pack
workflows.dek: Four tiles became a panel Android Police's Jon Gilbert minimizes the tile size so a long press opens each tile's secondary action, removes the ones never tapped (Alarm, Wallet, Device controls, Cast), adds the native TV remote, Focus mode, and VPN tiles, installs the free Toolkit Tiles app for everything Android does not ship, and hands the multi-step routines to MacroDroid or Tasker, with the result reported honestly: the Temperature tile refused to work and the Level stopped after a few seconds on a Pixel 10 Pro, while both behaved on a Galaxy Tab S9 FE.

workflows.title: Ask Gemini to summarize a chat into Google Keep, and the answer you needed months later is findable again
workflows.dek: Save it where search works Android Police's Anu Joy switches on Google Workspace under Gemini's Personal Intelligence, Connected Apps, closes a useful conversation by typing Summarize this chat and add it to Google Keep, and gets a Keep note of the key points carrying a Gemini tag that links back to the original thread, then searches Keep rather than the chat list later, because asking Gemini to hunt through its own history went in the wrong direction and came back saying it could not find anything.
needs: Google Workspace as a connected app

workflows.title: MakeUseOf swapped four security subscriptions for free tools, and the three quoted prices came to about $315 a year
workflows.dek: Four renewals audited Microsoft Defender takes the antivirus slot on Windows, KeePassXC takes the password slot at $35.88 a year saved, WireGuard takes the VPN slot for reaching your own network, and Restic takes backup, with the cost of each swap stated plainly: you now own the syncing, the storage, and the restore test.
needs: Somewhere of your own to back up

workflows.title: Three Raycast features a Windows user can set up free tonight: snippets, quicklinks, and the extension store
workflows.dek: Included in the free plan XDA's Hamlin Rozario saves repeated blocks of text as snippets that expand with dynamic placeholders for the date, the time, and the clipboard, builds quicklinks that jump to a site, file, folder, or a search inside an app, and installs community extensions for Notion, Slack, Spotify, and 1Password from inside the launcher, while the AI pieces (Screen Awareness, Quick AI, and Quick Fix) need Raycast Pro, listed on the official pricing page at $10 a month or $96 a year.
needs: The sites and folders you reopen

workflows.title: Set Private DNS before your next hotel or cafe Wi-Fi, and the network stops seeing which sites you open
workflows.dek: One Android setting How-To Geek's Arol Wright switches Private DNS to a named provider hostname, dns.google, one.one.one.one, dns.quad9.net, or dns.adguard-dns.com, which wraps every lookup in the same kind of encryption that protects HTTPS websites, though the piece is equally plain that it does not hide your IP address, it is no substitute for a VPN, and some hotel and corporate networks block the port it relies on and drop you back to unencrypted DNS.

workflows.title: Photograph the cards you keep losing, and Google Wallet turns them into passes you can reach from the lock screen
workflows.dek: Everything else, tapped Android Police's Anu Joy opens Google Wallet, taps the plus for Add to Wallet, chooses Everything else, photographs or picks an image of a library card, gym membership, insurance slip, or hotel confirmation, corrects whatever the scan misread, and gives it a name, marking the sensitive ones private so they need biometric unlock, with the limit stated outright: a photographed pass is not an official replacement for the document you still have to carry.

workflows.title: Six things your Android phone already remembers for you, from dismissed notifications to where you parked
workflows.dek: Switch on notification history MakeUseOf's Oluwademilade Afolabi turns on Settings, Notifications, Notification history, shares a saved Wi-Fi network by QR code from its own page, keeps Google Maps Timeline as the record of where the phone has been, pulls older copies from the keyboard's clipboard, checks Now Playing history on a Pixel, and saves the parking marker with a note for the garage level, with the catch that notification history holds nothing from before you switch it on.

workflows.title: Report phishing, write a strict filter, block a whole domain, and keep a blocklist to thin the scam mail
workflows.dek: Four settings deep Gmail's phishing report, a custom filter built from sender or subject or keyword, a wildcard block written as the domain rather than one address, and the blocklist each cut a different slice of junk before you ever read it.

workflows.title: Length beats punctuation: four to six random words make a better password than a clever symbol
workflows.dek: Twenty characters up NIST's digital identity guidelines no longer recommend mandatory composition rules, so the piece builds passphrases of 20 to 30 characters, or four to six random words, stores them in a manager, and puts multi-factor on top.
needs: Four to six random words each

workflows.title: Clean up a Windows PC with WinGet: list what shipped, uninstall the bloat, then upgrade the rest in one command
workflows.dek: Five commands total winget list shows everything installed, winget show explains an unfamiliar entry, winget uninstall removes it in seconds, and winget upgrade --all updates what remains, though protected components such as Microsoft Edge will not go.
needs: The app IDs from winget list

workflows.title: Three formula habits are what make Excel crawl: volatile functions, legacy array formulas, and VLOOKUP
workflows.dek: Swap three things Type the date instead of leaving NOW, TODAY, RAND, or INDIRECT to recalculate on every edit, retire the Ctrl+Shift+Enter array formulas for helper columns or dynamic arrays, and move VLOOKUP and HLOOKUP to XLOOKUP.
needs: A workbook that has grown slow

workflows.title: Excel's LET function names the pieces inside a monster formula, so next month you can still read it
workflows.dek: Name it once How-To Geek's Tony Phillips rebuilds a sprawling salesperson scoring formula by giving each part a name, revenue from SUMIFS, target from MAXIFS, profit from SUMIFS, and rating from AVERAGEIFS, then stacking targetScore, profitMargin, and ratingScore on top of them, which also stops the same revenue figure from being calculated twice, though LET needs Microsoft 365, Excel 2024, Excel 2021, or Excel for the web, and separate helper cells are still the better answer when a middle value has to feed a chart or a PivotTable.

workflows.title: One renamed desktop folder opens every Windows control in a single scrolling list
workflows.dek: Rename a new folder MakeUseOf's Suman Biswas right clicks the desktop, makes a folder, and renames it GodMode.{ED7BA470-8E54-465E-825C-99712043E01C}, which turns it into a Control Panel style icon holding more than 30 grouped sections, Administrative Tools, Backup and Restore, Devices and Printers, Power Options, Windows Defender Firewall and the rest, searchable in one list and free of the Settings app's ads, though it wants an administrator account and reaches nothing that Settings or Control Panel could not already reach the slow way.

workflows.title: Four ordinary habits are burning through your SSD's write cycles, and each one has a quick fix
workflows.dek: Four quiet drains XDA's Abhishek Kumar Mishra turns off Fast Startup in Control Panel because every shutdown writes a little data to the drive, keeps 15 to 20 percent of the disk free so it is not endlessly shuffling blocks, sends big repeated writes like downloads and virtual machines to a cheap external scratch SSD instead of the boot drive, and reins in the quiet background writers: search indexing, cloud sync folders, the paging file, and telemetry.
needs: A Windows PC with an SSD
An external drive for big files

workflows.title: Waze reads every hazard report aloud, and one settings page turns the chatter down without losing the map
workflows.dek: Keep the map, mute the voice How-To Geek's Adam Davidson opens Settings, Driving Preferences, Alerts and Reports, Reports, and for a category such as Vehicle on shoulder leaves Show on Map switched on while turning Alert while Driving off, so the warning still appears on screen without cutting into music or an audiobook, with the limits stated plainly: the change applies to every future trip rather than one drive, related hazards are grouped so a pothole cannot be silenced on its own, and undoing it means the same walk back through the menu.

workflows.title: Six Wi-Fi changes that made the biggest difference: band steering, narrower channels, and a wired mesh backhaul
workflows.dek: Six that held up Band steering hands each device to the band that suits it, a narrower channel width reduces overlap with the neighbors instead of chasing 160MHz, the desktop and printer and cameras move to Ethernet, the mesh point sits between the router and the dead zone with a wired backhaul, and the old signal repeating extender comes out of the wall.
needs: An hour to test as you go

workflows.title: Windows 11 may have quietly encrypted your drive, so find the recovery key before the next firmware update
workflows.dek: Check before you update XDA's Abhinav Raj writes that Device Encryption turns itself on for compatible Windows 11 24H2 clean installs and resets, that Settings then Privacy and Security then Device Encryption shows the status, that the recovery key is backed up automatically only when you sign in with a Microsoft, work, or school account, and that a local account holder should never assume a copy is waiting in the cloud.
needs: Somewhere safe to keep the key

workflows.title: Excel's What-If Analysis menu holds three tools that retire guesswork: Data Tables, Scenario Manager, and Goal Seek
workflows.dek: Data, then Forecast MakeUseOf's Adaeze Uche runs a 500,000 dollar mortgage at 5.0% over 360 months through a Data Table to see many payments at once, saves named revenue cases in Scenario Manager for a side by side summary sheet, and works Goal Seek backward from a 500 dollar monthly payment budget, with the honest warning that large Data Tables recalculate on every worksheet change and slow the file down.
needs: A sheet with a real formula
The inputs you want to test

workflows.title: Five Google Calendar habits worth building, from a daily agenda email to a bookable appointment page
workflows.dek: Five small setups Android Police's Anu Joy taps an empty slot and picks Task so Google Tasks items live in the grid, switches Daily agenda from None to Email under Settings for my calendars on desktop, sets events to repeat rather than retyping them, turns a message into an event from Gmail's three dot menu, and publishes an appointment schedule with buffer time and conflict checks.

workflows.title: Windows has been sampling your typing and handwriting since setup, and two toggles turn it off
workflows.dek: Two switches and a dictionary How-To Geek's Tony Phillips points to Settings, Privacy and security, Diagnostics and feedback, where Improve inking and typing sends Microsoft samples of what you write for prediction and spelling work, and then to Inking and typing personalization, where the customized dictionary is built from your own typing history and clearing it is the price of switching it off.

workflows.title: Point Excel's Power Query at a folder once, and next month's report rebuilds itself on one Refresh All
workflows.dek: Aim it at the folder Get Data then From Folder reads every file in one pass, Combine and Transform Data stacks them, Unpivot Other Columns turns a wide layout into vertical rows, and Close and Load drops the finished table in, so next month is a matter of adding files and clicking Refresh All.
needs: A report you rebuild by hand

workflows.title: Six things worth scanning with Google Lens, from appliance serial numbers to laundry care symbols
workflows.dek: Stop retyping fine print How-To Geek lifts model and serial numbers off appliances for parts and warranty lookups, copies the Wi-Fi password from a router label without typos, reads tiny ingredient lists and taps through to nutrition and allergy detail, decodes laundry care symbols, prices unfamiliar thrift finds, and turns handwriting into searchable text, though messy writing and poor light still defeat it.

workflows.title: Turn off the three places Windows 11 advertises to you: Start, the lock screen, and notifications
workflows.dek: Three settings panes Personalization then Start hides recommendations for tips, shortcuts, and new apps while Privacy and security then Search turns off search highlights, Personalization then Lock screen drops the fun facts once the background is a picture or slideshow, and Privacy and security then Recommendations and offers plus System then Notifications end the OneDrive, Microsoft 365, Edge, and Copilot nudges.

workflows.title: Set Storage Sense to run every month instead of waiting for the disk to fill up
workflows.dek: Change the schedule XDA's writer moved Storage Sense off its default of during low free disk space, set it to every month, ran it once by hand, and recovered about 30GB on a 2TB drive that still had more than 700GB free, while leaving the Downloads cleanup switched off so old IDs, resumes, and invoices are not swept away.

workflows.title: Build an Obsidian knowledge base out of old exports, voice memos, and PDFs instead of typing new notes
workflows.dek: Import, record, drop in The Importer plugin pulls in Google Keep notes exported through Google Takeout along with Markdown from apps like Joplin or JotterPad, the Audio Recorder core plugin under Settings then Core Plugins captures spoken notes while you read or after a meeting, and PDFs join the vault by dragging them in on desktop or tapping the paperclip on mobile.

workflows.title: Speak into Google Keep and let Keep Live turn a rambling list into a structured note
workflows.dek: Say it, then tap Done Keep Live listens while you describe what you need, such as the documents for a passport renewal, structures the result into a note, and accepts follow-ups like splitting an itinerary into two notes or adding to an existing one, though a split leaves the original behind and you cannot ask it to set a reminder.

workflows.title: Give MacroDroid three standing rules and stop toggling Wi-Fi, opening maps, and silencing your phone by hand
workflows.dek: Trigger, action, constraint A geofence switches Wi-Fi and mobile data as you arrive home and leave it, an Android Auto connection opens YouTube Music and navigation toward work, and a calendar event mutes the phone and restores the sound when the meeting ends.

workflows.title: Three Excel functions that retire manual filtering: XLOOKUP, SUMIFS with COUNTIFS, and FILTER
workflows.dek: Stop counting columns XLOOKUP asks only what to find, where to look, and what to return, SUMIFS and COUNTIFS total or count rows against as many as 127 criteria pairs while leaving the source data untouched, and FILTER returns every matching row from one formula and updates itself when the data changes.
needs: A sheet you filter by hand

workflows.title: Five Excel habits to drop tonight: merged cells, blank rows, hand-applied colors, hard-coded rates, one crowded sheet
workflows.dek: Unmerge first Complete records replace merged cells and blank rows, conditional formatting replaces hand-applied color, changeable values move into their own referenced cells, and one file becomes three tabs for source, logic, and report.

workflows.title: Let one formula do the dragging: MAP, BYROW, BYCOL, SCAN, and REDUCE retire your helper columns
workflows.dek: One cell, one formula MAP works across matching arrays, BYROW and BYCOL handle a whole row or column at once, SCAN keeps every running subtotal, and REDUCE returns only the final accumulated answer.
needs: Excel with MAP, SCAN, and REDUCE
A sheet full of dragged formulas
Room outside a table for spills

workflows.title: Swap four built-in Windows tools for free alternatives and stop waiting on search, Explorer, and Start
workflows.dek: Four swaps, one evening Everything reads the Master File Table for fast file lookup, Files adds dual panes and file tagging, AppControl keeps three days of performance history, and PowerToys Command Palette stands in for the Start menu.
needs: Files costs $8 on the Store, free direct

workflows.title: Turn off one Chrome setting on your phone and get back roughly 1.5 to 2 hours of daily battery
workflows.dek: Stop the prefetching Preload pages, under Settings then Privacy and security, keeps guessing which links you will tap and holding the radio awake, and Android Police puts switching it off at roughly 1.5 to 2 hours of extra daily battery for heavy browsers, at the cost of slower page loads.
needs: Two days to judge the difference

workflows.title: Put your cameras, speakers, and TVs on the guest network, then test that the wall actually holds
workflows.dek: Guests optional Smart devices get internet without a path to your files, but isolation is two separate switches, so try reaching your home server from the guest side before you trust it.
needs: A router with a guest network

workflows.title: Four Android settings quietly hold your notifications back, and switching each one off brings them on time
workflows.dek: Battery saver first Battery Saver, per-app battery optimization, Data Saver, and the pause-unused-apps toggle each throttle background sync, and How-To Geek gives the menu path to reverse all four for the apps that actually matter.
needs: Your short list of urgent apps

workflows.title: Give Gemini standing instructions and a few saved Gems so you stop re-explaining yourself every session
workflows.dek: Tell it once Standing notes under Settings, then Personal Intelligence, plus connected Google apps and a couple of saved Gems, stop you retyping the same background into every new conversation.

workflows.title: Android will now move your saved passwords and passkeys into a new manager in a few seconds
workflows.dek: Import, never retype A new transfer flow carries passwords and passkeys between Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden, and Dashlane, skipping duplicates as it goes, with more partners said to follow.
needs: A screen lock on the phone

workflows.title: Write in plain Markdown and let one free Pandoc command hand back the Word file people asked for
workflows.dek: One command out Draft where you like, then run pandoc article.md -o article.docx to produce the .docx a colleague or client wanted, with templates available when the default styling is not enough.

workflows.title: Turn on Chrome's Memory Saver and a 16 tab session drops from about 6GB of RAM to about 2GB
workflows.dek: Settings, then Performance MakeUseOf's Oluwademilade Afolabi, writing on September 9, chooses Maximum from the three Memory Saver modes, which also offer Moderate and Balanced. Across 16 tabs spanning YouTube, Gmail, Google Docs, Reddit, shopping pages, and articles, he watched memory use fall from roughly 6GB to roughly 2GB with nothing missing from the tab bar. Sleeping tabs reload briefly when you return to them, and he notes that complex web applications holding a session may not restore cleanly, which is what the Always keep these sites active list on the same page is for.
needs: A list of tabs to keep awake

workflows.title: Close Gemini's door to your Gmail with one connector switch and one opt-out buried in Gmail
workflows.dek: Two settings, both hidden How-To Geek's Vishwamoorthy Ramakrishnan, writing on September 9, starts in the Gemini app: Profile, then Personal Intelligence, then Connected Apps, then Google Workspace, where disabling the connector also disconnects Drive, Docs, and Keep, because Google offers no per app control. The second setting lives in the Gmail app under Settings, your Gmail account, then Google Workspace Smart Features, where Smart Features in Google Workspace is opt out rather than opt in; he found it switched on automatically across several accounts. His closing limit is worth keeping: pasting an email into a Gemini chat still shares it, and such chats may be subject to review by human annotators.

workflows.title: Stop Chrome from running in the background after you close it and take back about 500MB on Windows
workflows.dek: One switch under System MakeUseOf's Brandon Miniman, writing on September 9, found Chrome still holding more than 1GB of RAM in background processes after he had closed it. The three dot menu, then Settings, then System, holds the toggle for continuing to run background apps when Chrome is closed; it ships on by default in Windows, and switching it off dropped his idle usage to 510MB, a reduction of 51%. Two caveats: the setting is Windows only, so Mac users will not find it, and with background apps off, website notifications may arrive late while Chrome is shut.

workflows.title: Install the Claude add-in inside PowerPoint and let the first draft of a deck build itself
workflows.dek: Add-ins, then Ctrl Alt C XDA's Parth Shah, writing on September 9, spends about two minutes on setup: open PowerPoint, go to Home and then Add-ins, search for Claude for Microsoft 365, install it (Microsoft AppSource carries it too), sign in with a Claude account, and call it up with Ctrl, Alt, and C on Windows. From there he builds most of a deck from a single prompt, repairs weak slides, improves layouts, and summarizes a presentation without leaving the app. The caveats are the account and the finish line: full functionality expects a Claude subscription, and Shah reckons the result is about 80% of the way there in minutes, leaving animations, visual polish, and the final details to you.

workflows.title: Six charging habits that left one Android phone at 88% battery health after two and a half years
workflows.dek: One setting, then five habits MakeUseOf's Varun Krishan, writing on September 9, credits a 12% decline over two and a half years to Settings, then Battery, then Battery health, then Charging optimization, where he turns on charging optimization and selects Limit to 80%, since lithium ion cells take more stress toward the top of their range. He leaves adaptive charging on so the phone learns when he unplugs and delays the last stretch of the charge until then. The remaining four are habits rather than switches: keep the phone off heavy work and off heat while charging, slip the case off when it runs warm, do not make a practice of draining to zero, save fast charging for when the clock demands it, and keep Android updated for its power management improvements.

workflows.title: Stop typing your card number into websites, and let a wallet or a virtual card stand in for it
workflows.dek: A token, not the digits MakeUseOf's Bertel King, writing on September 8, splits the job in two. In a store, paying from Apple Pay, Google Wallet, or Samsung Wallet hands the terminal a virtual token instead of your actual card number, using cards you already own and costing nothing extra. Online, where he notes many websites still will not take a wallet, he reaches for a virtual card service such as Privacy.com and generates a single-use or merchant-locked number, so a breach at one store cannot travel. PayPal is his fallback for the degree of separation it provides, with the honest limit that it is not accepted everywhere and specifically not at Amazon. He cites Visa figures putting tokenized payments at a 30 percent reduction in online fraud and as much as 90 percent against some point-of-sale fraud.
needs: A phone with a wallet app
A virtual card service for online

workflows.title: Add a slicer, a timeline, and a PivotChart, and a PivotTable becomes a dashboard you click
workflows.dek: Three commands, one dashboard How-To Geek's Tony Phillips, writing on September 8, stays inside a single Excel menu. PivotTable Analyze and then Insert Slicer turns a field such as Salesperson into a row of clickable buttons that replace the filter dropdown, and Report Connections wires one slicer to several PivotTables at once. PivotTable Analyze and then Insert Timeline does the same for a date field, so, as he puts it, instead of opening a filter menu and selecting individual dates, I can simply click a month or drag across several months. PivotTable Analyze and then PivotChart adds the picture, and because all three stay connected, moving one control updates the table and the chart together.
needs: A data table with a date column

workflows.title: Seven Android settings worth switching on before a new phone ever joins your Wi-Fi
workflows.dek: Setup night, once Android Police's Jade Bryan Jardinico, writing on September 6, works down a setup checklist. Under Security and privacy, then Lost device protection and Theft protection, he turns on Theft Detection Lock, considers Offline Device Lock, and confirms Remote Lock so a lost phone can be locked from android.com/lock. More security and privacy holds Unknown tracker alerts for stray Bluetooth trackers, and Mobile network security, where he enables network security notifications and checks that Block 2G is on. Settings, System, Keyboard, Keyboard apps, Gboard, then Privacy is where he switches off the data sharing toggles, Privacy controls is where he stops passwords appearing on screen as they are typed, and System, Software updates is the last stop for both system and Google Play updates. One caveat a reader raised in the comments is fair: most of these are phone security settings rather than Wi-Fi settings, whatever the headline says.
needs: A Google account for remote lock

workflows.title: Three Google Maps settings to turn off: Timeline, automatic offline maps, and visual search ads
workflows.dek: Three buried toggles Android Police's Akshay Bhalla, writing on September 6, digs out the settings Google does not surface. Your profile icon, then Your Timeline, then Location and privacy settings, then Timeline is where background location history lives, and he notes that switching it off does not cost you personalized recommendations, with a three month auto-delete offered as the middle path. Profile, then Offline maps, then the gear icon is where he turns off auto-update offline maps and auto-download recommended maps or restricts them to Wi-Fi only, because he says they can drain battery, fill storage, and burn through data. The third lives outside Maps entirely, in your Google Account under Data and privacy, then Web and App Activity, where unchecking Include Visual Search History stops those images feeding personalized ads.
needs: Five minutes and a search box

workflows.title: Turn your router's transmit power down to about half, and a crowded home Wi-Fi network gets steadier
workflows.dek: One setting, then restart MakeUseOf's Oliver Haslam, writing on September 7, sends you to Transmit Power Control, usually filed under Advanced Wireless Settings once you sign in to the router at 192.168.0.1 or 10.0.0.1, and recommends Medium or about the 50% mark instead of maximum. His reasoning is that a router at full power drowns out the small antennas in phones and smart home devices, bounces echoes off hard surfaces indoors, forces neighboring networks into Co-Channel Interference that makes them pause, and keeps devices locked onto the loudest signal rather than roaming to a nearer access point. The article's images show TP-Link, Netgear Orbi, ASUS, and GL.iNet gear, and he says to restart the router afterward and let things settle. One thing the article does not do is weigh the trade: it names no downside to lowering power, so walk to your weakest room after the change and step back up a notch if coverage there suffers.
needs: Your router's admin page and password

workflows.title: Seven Windows shortcuts that replace the mouse trips you make in File Explorer all day
workflows.dek: Learn two, then two more XDA's Tanveer Singh, writing on September 7, lists the seven he wishes he had known sooner. Win and E opens a fresh File Explorer window without hunting for the taskbar icon. Backspace moves up one folder, Alt with the left and right arrows retrace and advance along the exact path you took, and Alt with the up arrow jumps to the parent folder. Alt and Enter opens Properties for whatever is selected, which he says changes the game once it replaces the right-click. Holding Shift while clicking a taskbar icon, or clicking it with the scroll wheel, opens a second instance of an app, and holding Ctrl and Shift as you launch one starts it as administrator. Win and comma peeks at the desktop while every window stays exactly where it is, and Win with the up arrow maximizes the active window.

workflows.title: Strip the Windows 11 taskbar and Start menu back to the parts you actually use
workflows.dek: Four toggles, then four more MakeUseOf's Gregory Gibson, writing on September 6, works through Settings in order. Under Personalization and then Taskbar he switches off Search, Task View, Widgets, and Resume. Under Personalization and then Start he turns off recently added apps, recommended files, tips, and suggestions. Under Privacy and security, then Search permissions, he disables Search highlights, and to stop web suggestions inside the Start menu he adds a DisableSearchBoxSuggestions value from Windows Terminal, which is the one step that edits the registry and deserves a careful hand. He reports less visual clutter and better responsiveness on a slow connection, and keeps what he removed on the keyboard instead: Win and S for search, Win and Tab for Task View.
needs: Windows Terminal for the last step

workflows.title: Open a second window on the same Excel workbook and let Alt and Tab do the sheet switching
workflows.dek: View, then New Window How-To Geek's Tony Phillips, writing on September 7, stopped fighting his habit of reaching for Alt and Tab and made Excel fit it instead.
