Click View and then New Window, and Excel opens a second window onto the same workbook rather than a copy: the title bar labels them with the file name followed by a 1 and a 2, and an edit made in either window saves to the one file. That turns Alt and Tab into a worksheet switcher, which he finds far less tedious than pressing Ctrl with Page Up or Page Down when the two sheets sit several tabs apart. He points to Excel's Watch Window as the alternative for the narrower job of keeping an eye on a few selected cells without moving between sheets at all.
needs: The View tab on the ribbon

workflows.title: Set up a new computer with five open source browser extensions before you install anything else
workflows.dek: Five installs, one afternoon XDA's Yash Patel, writing on September 6, treats a fresh browser as the real setup job and fills it with five open source extensions that each carry their own weight. Bitwarden generates a strong password and stores it, so the vault starts clean instead of inheriting years of reused logins. Dark Reader applies dark mode to sites that lack one, with brightness, contrast, and sepia sliders, and he leaves it switched off on the sites whose own dark mode is already decent. Privacy Badger blocks third-party trackers by watching tracking behavior rather than trying to break every site feature. Zotero Connector saves an article and pulls the title, author, and publication details along with it, which is an academic tool he repurposed for ordinary reading. Tabox saves a whole browsing session as a collection in one click, so a research tab pile can be closed and reopened later. Patel describes all five as open source; the article does not give prices, so check each store listing before you commit.
needs: A Chrome, Edge, or Firefox browser

workflows.title: Audit which Android apps run in the background, then cut their data and location, and get the standby battery back
workflows.dek: Look first, then restrict Android Police's Ali Salman Zia, writing on September 6, starts in Settings, Battery, Battery usage, sorts the list to find the heaviest apps, and then walks each one through Settings, Apps, the app name, Mobile data and Wi-Fi, switching off background data for anything with no legitimate reason to be awake. He ended up restricting roughly 90 percent of his installed apps, and reports his overnight standby drain falling from about half the battery to about a quarter. Two caveats matter before you copy him. Most messaging and social apps deliver notifications over Firebase Cloud Messaging, a shared connection Google Play Services keeps open regardless of an app's background data setting, so alerts largely survive, but weather widgets stopped refreshing on their own and cloud backups paused until he opened those apps by hand. The bigger win, he says, was not the data restriction at all: cutting background location access for apps that did not need it added more hours than the data change did.
needs: A list of apps you rarely open

workflows.title: Build one bootable USB stick that carries ten free repair tools, and stop rebuilding it every time a PC breaks
workflows.dek: Ventoy once, ISOs forever XDA's Abhishek Kumar Mishra, writing on September 6, makes the case for one drive instead of a shoebox of them. Ventoy turns a USB stick into a multi-boot device once, and after that you copy ISO files onto it like ordinary files and pick from a menu at boot, with no reformatting and no rebuilding the stick for each new tool. His ten are Ventoy itself, a Windows 11 installer, MX Linux, Netboot.xyz for pulling an operating system down on demand, Hiren's BootCD PE and System Rescue for Windows and Linux troubleshooting, Clonezilla for cloning a drive, GParted Live for partitions, MemTest86 for suspect RAM, and ShredOS for wiping a disk before it leaves the house, with Kaspersky Rescue Disk as an optional addition. Two limits to plan around: Netboot.xyz needs a working internet connection over Ethernet, and a secure wipe can run for hours or even a day depending on the method you pick. Mishra is also clear that this is his selection, not a canonical list.
needs: The ISO files you want on it

workflows.title: Turn off hibernation on a desktop PC and take back several gigabytes of Windows storage in one command
workflows.dek: One command, one file XDA's Hamlin Rozario, writing on September 6, points at hiberfil.sys, the hidden file Windows 11 keeps so it can write the contents of RAM to disk before hibernating. Open Command Prompt as an administrator, run powercfg /hibernate off, and the file goes away; fsutil volume diskfree C: before and after shows exactly what you got back. The file runs about 40 percent of installed RAM, which on his 64GB machine meant a little over 25GB, and works out to roughly 12GB on a 32GB system and 6GB on a 16GB one. The trade is stated plainly: Fast Startup uses the same file, so a normal boot will take a few seconds longer, and hibernation is genuinely useful on a laptop, which is why he frames this as a desktop move. If you want most of the space without losing Fast Startup, powercfg /hibernate /type reduced shrinks the file to about 20 percent of RAM instead of deleting it.

workflows.title: Let Google Maps send your live ETA to whoever is waiting, instead of texting from the driver's seat
workflows.dek: Swipe up, then share How-To Geek's Jorge A. Aguilar, writing on September 5, starts navigation the usual way, then swipes up on the card at the bottom of the screen that shows the ETA and the distance, and taps Share trip progress. Recipients come from Google contacts, or the link goes out through iMessage, WhatsApp, or Messenger, and what they see is a live map with the route on it, an ETA that recalculates when traffic reroutes the drive, and the phone's battery level and charging status. Aguilar is clear about the one real limit: this exists only while turn-by-turn navigation is running, and it shuts itself off the moment the car reaches the destination, which is why he points anyone who wants continuous location sharing toward Apple's Find My instead.
needs: One contact to share it with

workflows.title: Put four extensions in Firefox for Android and delete the standalone apps they replace
workflows.dek: Menu, Extensions, Add MakeUseOf's Sagar Naresh, writing on September 5, installs extensions on the phone the way most people only do on a desktop: open Firefox for Android, open the menu, tap Extensions, search for the one you want, and tap Add to Firefox. Sink It for Reddit strips the Open in app banner and most of the ads from Reddit on the web, then adds color-coded comment threads, subreddit and word muting, and gesture-based upvoting. Firefox Relay generates random forwarding addresses inside the browser so a signup form never gets the real inbox. Read Aloud turns whatever is in the open tab into spoken audio in more than 40 languages, and Worldwide Radio streams from a catalog of nearly 50,000 stations. One honest note about the source: the headline promises five extensions and the article names four.
needs: A Mozilla account for Relay masks

workflows.title: Turn Obsidian daily notes into a second brain that keeps working when you stop maintaining it
workflows.dek: Capture first, organize later How-To Geek's Dibakar Ghosh, writing on September 5, starts with the Daily Notes core plugin switched on in Settings, writes into whatever page today opens, and drops placeholder links in double brackets around ideas he has not developed yet, which then show up in Graph View as unfilled nodes waiting for him. Omnisearch does the retrieval, ranking results by the BM25 algorithm with typo tolerance rather than listing every match, and it will reach into images and PDFs once the Text Extractor plugin is added. Calendar puts a month view in the right sidebar so any date opens its daily note without scrolling a folder list; Tag Wrangler shows every tag in one place so redundant ones can be renamed, merged, or deleted before tag drift sets in; and Tasks turns checkboxes typed in passing into real tasks with due dates and priorities, rendered across the vault from a code block.
needs: The Daily Notes core plugin on

workflows.title: Find out which Windows apps are eating the data plan, then cap them in Settings
workflows.dek: Look first, then cap How-To Geek's Dibakar Ghosh starts at Settings, Network and internet, Advanced network settings, Data usage, which lists what every app pulled over the last 30 days; on his machine that was 204.8GB total, with System and Windows Update at 93GB and the Brave browser at 74.16GB. From there he closes the taps one at a time: Settings, Apps, Installed apps, then Advanced options and Background app permissions set to Never, which he is careful to say works only for Microsoft Store and built-in Windows apps rather than traditionally installed EXE software; marking the connection as metered; pausing updates for up to five weeks; and capping update bandwidth under Settings, Windows Update, Advanced options, Delivery optimization, as either an absolute Mbps figure or a percentage he sets to 30. For anything that ignores all of that, he reaches for Portmaster, a free and open-source application firewall that shows connections per app and can cut one off the internet entirely.

workflows.title: Sync one Obsidian vault between a PC and an Android phone without paying for sync
workflows.dek: Drive on one side, Autosync on the other MakeUseOf's Tashreef Shareef keeps his notes on every device without the 4 to 5 dollars a month Obsidian Sync would cost, and the trick is that an Obsidian vault is just a folder of markdown files. On the computer he installs Google Drive for desktop, turns on Mirror files in its preferences so the folder lives locally as well as in the cloud, moves the vault inside it, and waits for the first sync to finish. On the phone he installs Autosync for Google Drive, connects the same account, creates a folder pair set to two way, switches on hidden file syncing so the .obsidian settings folder travels too, and then opens the synced DriveSyncFiles folder as the vault in the Obsidian app. He is straight about the tradeoffs: edit on one device at a time, let the sync land before switching, and accept that there is no end to end encryption here, so Google can technically read the files.

workflows.title: Connect Gemini to Slides, Sheets, Keep, and YouTube Music, and stop doing the setup work
workflows.dek: Four apps, one assistant Android Police's Parth Shah, writing on September 3, connects Gemini to four Google apps he already had open. In Slides the Gemini icon sits in the upper right corner and builds a deck from a written prompt, with a Help me Visualize panel for on-brand images; he advises doing this in the Slides web app rather than in Canvas, because the result is easier to customize afterward. YouTube Music is reached by typing @YouTubeMusic inside a Gemini chat and describing the playlist you want, down to a request such as low-fi beats with no lyrics, strictly under 80 BPM, though playlist creation is limited to the mobile apps for now. Sheets opens from the sidebar and writes complex formulas, builds pivot tables and charts, summarizes a sheet, and pulls data across files, with the caveat that full Workspace integration needs a premium Gemini plan. Keep builds categorized lists from a prompt and pulls facts back out of notes you already wrote.
needs: The Gemini app or web app

workflows.title: Ask a chatbot for one self-contained HTML file and get a desktop toolbox that needs no install
workflows.dek: One prompt, one file How-To Geek's Tony Phillips gave Gemini and Claude the same detailed prompt on September 4: build 14 small utilities, sticky notes, a text cleaner, a word counter, date and time calculators, a timezone converter, a stopwatch, a countdown timer, unit and file size converters, percentage and loan calculators, a random generator, and a URL cleaner, all inside a single self-contained HTML file with no external resources. You paste the result into Notepad, save it, and open it in a browser; there is no installation, no coding knowledge, and no internet connection required once the file exists. Gemini finished in about two minutes and Claude in about six. The reason to test before trusting is in his results: Gemini's timezone converter turned 3 p.m. in New York into 3 p.m. in London instead of 8 p.m., which Phillips calls a serious problem for a tool whose whole job is converting times, while Claude's version got it right.

workflows.title: Try Android's built-in quiet mode for two weeks before you spend $300 on a dumbphone
workflows.dek: Focus Mode, then bedtime Android Police's Ali Salman Zia was close to buying a Light Phone before working through the Digital Wellbeing settings already on the phone: Focus Mode pauses the apps you name, greys their icons on the home screen so they cannot be opened until the mode is off, and can run on a schedule; Bedtime Mode switches the screen to grayscale at a set hour, mutes notifications, and dims the wallpaper, taking away the color the apps were counting on; App Timers cap daily minutes per app; and Do Not Disturb quiets notifications without blocking the apps themselves. He finishes at the home screen, hiding icons, removing widgets, and dropping to a single column, and his caveat is the honest one: every distracting app is still installed and one setting away, so this is discipline with help rather than hardware, which is exactly why he suggests two weeks of it before any money changes hands.

workflows.title: Turn OneNote into one command center with a dashboard page, custom tags, and a tag summary
workflows.dek: One page rules the rest XDA's Parth Shah organizes notebooks, section groups, and sections around what he calls operational pillars rather than by stray thought, then builds a single master dashboard page whose internal page links jump straight to active drafts, weekly priorities, and key resources, so the daily navigation cost mostly disappears. The part worth copying is the tagging: past the default checkbox he adds custom tags such as High Priority and Waiting on Reply plus project-specific ones, and OneNote's Tag Summary then pulls every tagged line from every notebook into one clean sidebar. He also sketches mind maps on an iPad with the Apple Pencil before typing them up on the desktop, and points Copilot Notebooks at chosen pages and OneDrive documents so questions are answered from his own notes; the write-up lists no drawbacks at all, so treat those last two as optional extras rather than requirements.
needs: OneNote and a notebook you use
One page to act as the dashboard
A short list of custom tags

workflows.title: Argue with Claude instead of agreeing with it, and brainstorming stops returning safe answers
workflows.dek: Pick the worst idea first MakeUseOf's Saikat Basu opens by asking for a whole spectrum of possibilities, explicitly including some that sound impractical, boring, weird, or commercially questionable, then does the opposite of what most people do: he picks the idea he finds least convincing and pushes back on it rather than asking for it to be improved. From there he challenges the assumption underneath, asking what a customer might actually want past the surface product, follows the branches the conversation wanders into instead of steering back, and treats each answer as a trigger for his own reaction rather than a finished result. His caveat should be read before you try it, because this method deliberately trades accuracy for strangeness and he says a little hallucination is acceptable here, which makes it a tool for generating ideas and never for facts you intend to rely on.
needs: A real problem worth arguing over

workflows.title: Five Google Keep features worth switching on: OCR, shared notes, the Gmail sidebar, voice, and labels
workflows.dek: Five settings, ten minutes How-To Geek's Sanya Shah starts with the Google Lens text recognition built into Keep, which lifts the words out of a photographed recipe, document, or menu and makes them editable and searchable instead of retyped; then shared notes, which let two people edit the same vacation plan, recipe, or shopping list at once rather than trading screenshots, which is how she and her spouse run theirs. A sidebar shortcut inside Gmail saves an important email straight into a Keep note, easier to find later than the same message buried in the inbox; voice capture transcribes what you say while cooking or commuting and lets you delete the audio while keeping the text; and labels such as Work, Recipes, Travel, and Personal filter the pile from the search bar. One caveat comes from her commenters rather than the article: the Gmail-to-Keep shortcut is a desktop sidebar feature and is not in the mobile app.
needs: Google Keep on phone and web

workflows.title: Turn Obsidian into a project tracker with the Tasks plugin and one dashboard note
workflows.dek: One plugin, one dashboard How-To Geek's Dibakar Ghosh installs the Tasks plugin from the obsidian-tasks-group, and every checkbox in the vault becomes a real task that can carry a due date, a start date, a scheduled date, one of six priority levels, an ID, a dependency on another task, a recurrence rule, a status of todo, in progress, done, or cancelled, and inline tags. Tasks then get written wherever the thought arrives, inside a daily note, a web clipping, or a project note, rather than in a dedicated tasks space, and one dashboard note holds code blocks whose filters pull them all back together, sorted by urgency, narrowed to what is blocked, or grouped by folder. Ghosh handed Claude the plugin's documentation so it writes the query syntax rather than memorizing it, syncs across devices with Syncthing instead of paying for Obsidian Sync, and reaches for CollabMD when a note needs real-time collaboration.
needs: One note to hold the dashboard
Syncthing if you want free sync

workflows.title: Stop engineering the perfect prompt and describe the outcome you actually want
workflows.dek: Say the goal, not the steps How-To Geek's Tony Phillips drops the long persona preamble and opens with the job itself, Look through this spreadsheet and tell me what looks wrong or needs fixing, then describes the result rather than the method, I need the solution to keep working when I add new transactions, instead of naming the Excel formulas it should use. The rest is conversational: let the model ask for what it still needs instead of front-loading every detail into the first message. Phillips points at OpenAI's own GPT-5.6 guidance, which encourages natural, goal-driven language over meticulously engineered wording, on the reasoning that the newer models infer the underlying goal from context.
needs: One real task, not a test

workflows.title: Seven jobs for the smart speaker gathering dust, starting with routines that need no voice
workflows.dek: Routines, sensors, geofences MakeUseOf's Bryan M. Wolfe starts in the routines section of the speaker's companion app, where a schedule can put the porch lights on at sunset or start the coffee maker at 6:45 AM, then moves to the triggers that need no voice at all: a geofence drawn around the house that locks the doors or turns off the lights when the radius is crossed, and motion or door sensors, priced under $15, that light an entryway for two minutes or announce that the dryer has finished. Many Amazon Echo and Google Nest Hub models carry Zigbee, so the speaker doubles as the hub for devices that cannot reach Wi-Fi by themselves; newer speakers keep critical routines such as unlocking a door or shutting off a heater running locally through an internet outage; and third-party links to weather, calendars, and fitness trackers let outside data start a routine on its own.

workflows.title: Four Excel tools hiding in the menus: Camera, Flash Fill, the Analysis ToolPak, and the Watch Window
workflows.dek: Four short menu dives MakeUseOf's Yadullah Abidi switches on the Camera tool from File, Options, Quick Access Toolbar with the list set to Commands Not in the Ribbon, and it drops a live picture of a cell range onto a sheet that updates itself whenever the source data changes, which is how a dashboard stops being a copy-paste chore; Flash Fill reads the pattern out of one example you type by hand and fills the rest of the column when you press Ctrl+E, or Command+E on a Mac; the Analysis ToolPak, enabled under File, Options, Add-ins with Manage set to Excel Add-ins, brings 19 statistical tools including regression, ANOVA, and histograms, though Abidi notes plainly that this add-in does not work in the web version; and the Watch Window, reached from the Formulas tab under Formula Auditing or with Alt+M+W, floats the few cells you actually need to keep an eye on while you work in another sheet entirely.
needs: Desktop Excel, not the web version
A workbook with real data in it

workflows.title: Five free tools that find the adware and spyware a Windows PC quietly picked up, in the order to run them
workflows.dek: Look, confirm, then clean MakeUseOf's Yadullah Abidi gives the sweep an order rather than a shopping list: start with Microsoft's Sysinternals pair, using Process Explorer to see what is running now, what each process has open, and which ones hold network connections under the TCP/IP tab of its properties, then Autoruns to read everything that starts itself, across services, scheduled tasks, DLLs, and registry entries; send anything suspicious from either tool to VirusTotal, which tests a file against more than 60 antivirus engines, and only then run a full scan with Malwarebytes, whose free version he finds catches adware that other scanners miss, or Spybot Search and Destroy for tracking software and keyloggers. He is careful about the limits: Process Explorer shows only current connections and not past ones, VirusTotal results are not definitive because engines disagree, most of Spybot's stronger features sit behind a paywall, and you should leave essential system processes and Microsoft-signed entries alone in Autoruns.
needs: An hour, and a slow hand

workflows.title: Replace the default apps on your phone one at a time, and keep only the swaps that earn their place
workflows.dek: One category at a time XDA's Abhishek Kumar Mishra worked through the apps that came on his phone and kept four replacements: VLC in place of Samsung's video player, because it handles formats the stock player struggles with, downloads subtitles, swaps audio tracks, and runs to 8x speed where the original stops at 2x; Microsoft's free SMS Organizer instead of Google Messages, which sorts messages into promotions, general, and banking, bolds one-time passcodes, and works offline with no Google account; and Niagara Launcher in place of One UI Home for a faster, vertical, far quieter home screen. Two of his notes matter as much as the picks: Microsoft is winding SMS Organizer down without naming a retirement date, so treat that one as temporary, and his fourth swap, self-hosting Bitwarden on a Raspberry Pi, needs technical setup that most readers should skip in favor of ordinary hosted Bitwarden.

workflows.title: Three ways to get wireless Android Auto, including in a car that has only ever offered the cable
workflows.dek: Pair, adapt, or add a screen How-To Geek's Nate Pangaro sorts the problem by what your car already has: if it supports wireless Android Auto natively, the whole job is opening the car's connection settings, choosing the car from Bluetooth on the phone, matching the six-digit code on both screens, and confirming Android Auto when it asks. If the car has wired Android Auto only, a dongle plugged into that same port does it, and he names the Aluratek AWCGD02F at $60 from Best Buy and the Motorola MA1, with generic units from around $50, warning that an adapter cannot add Android Auto to a car that never had it and that CarPlay-only adapters will not do. If the car has neither, a portable dashboard unit such as the Podofo screen at around $46 on Amazon works in any vehicle, suction-cupped to the dash, powered from the lighter socket, with audio over a 3.5mm cable or Bluetooth, at the cost of wires he admits end up all over the place.
needs: A car stereo, wired or wireless
About $50 if you need an adapter

workflows.title: Build a shared expense sheet that emails everyone their balance every Monday morning
workflows.dek: Six columns and one trigger Android Police's Irene Okpanachi keeps a People tab holding name, email, total paid, fair share, balance, and status, where SUMIF adds every expense recorded against a person in the paid-by column, fair share divides the total spending by the number of people, balance subtracts one from the other, and a single IF statement turns that number into who owes and who is owed; she had Gemini write the Apps Script, opened Extensions and then Apps Script from inside the sheet rather than on its own, picked sendBalanceReminders from the function dropdown, authorized it, and set a time-driven weekly trigger for Monday between 8am and 9am so the sheet asks once a week instead of constantly, and she is clear that a popup or ad blocker will quietly stop the trigger form from saving unless script.google.com is allowed through.
needs: One Sheet with a People tab
Apps Script, from the Extensions menu

workflows.title: Four free tools that give an aging Windows laptop back its disk space and its idle CPU
workflows.dek: Telemetry, bloat, temp files, search MakeUseOf's Digvijay Kumar works an old laptop in four passes: O&O ShutUp10++ gathers 319 toggles across its Current User and Local Machine tabs into one window, and applying only the recommended settings, which leave Windows Update and security protection alone, took his idle CPU from around 15% to 2%; Bulk Crap Uninstaller found 197 installed programs totaling over 23GB and drew a disk space map of them, and he skipped anything tied to system drivers before running its deep scan for stranded folders and registry entries; Microsoft PC Manager showed 9GB of temporary files and memory sitting at 80%, cleared it in seconds with the Boost button, and then stayed running quietly; and Everything indexed more than seventy-three thousand files in under a second by reading the NTFS USN Journal directly while holding memory to a few megabytes, after which he switched the Windows Search indexing service off entirely.
needs: O&O ShutUp10++ and Bulk Crap Uninstaller

workflows.title: Clear out the memories ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude have quietly been keeping about you
workflows.dek: Three settings panels Android Authority's Andrew Grush runs the same cleanup through all three assistants: in ChatGPT you open the profile icon, then Settings and Personalization, click Manage beside Memory Summary, and remove single entries with the trash icon, or use Clear ChatGPT's Memory at the bottom to reset the lot; in Claude you open Settings from the lower left sidebar, choose Memory, delete whole categories or simply ask in conversation for something to be forgotten, and untick Generate memory from chat history if you would rather pause it altogether; Gemini is the awkward one, handled under Settings and Gemini Apps Activity with the Delete dropdown set to All time, which Grush calls far from ideal because it means clearing whole chats rather than single memories, while Instructions for Gemini is where any standing rules you want kept should live.
needs: An account on any of the three
A few minutes in each app's settings
A note of any rules worth keeping

workflows.title: Five Google Maps features for a busy day, from a nine stop route to a parking pin that saves itself
workflows.dek: Plan the whole errand run How-To Geek's T.M. Amrita searches the first destination, taps Directions, then uses Add stop to chain on up to nine more and drags them into a sensible order with the two-line handle, which works for driving, walking, and cycling but not public transit; she saves places into custom lists from the bookmark icon under You, turns on Automatically save parking under Settings, Navigation, Parking options so a crowded lot stops being a memory test, checks Street View from the layers icon before visiting somewhere unfamiliar since blue-highlighted roads are the ones with coverage, and taps the trip panel mid-drive to Share trip progress so whoever is waiting at the airport can see the arrival time instead of texting for it.
needs: A Google account for saved lists

workflows.title: One standing instruction that tells Claude to assume and keep moving instead of stalling on questions
workflows.dek: Assume, then say so MakeUseOf's Saikat Basu adds one behavioral rule rather than a longer prompt, telling the assistant to answer directly and move the work forward, to make a reasonable assumption and briefly state it when something is missing, and to ask a follow-up only when the missing piece is genuinely necessary; he shows the three places it can live, in Claude's Settings under Profile Preferences for every chat, in Project Instructions for one kind of work, or pasted at the top of a single prompt, and he is careful to say this is not a blanket ban on questions, recommending the conditional version and steady refinement based on which assumptions it gets wrong.

workflows.title: Trust your phone as a level and a compass, and keep real hardware for everything you have to measure
workflows.dek: Two sensors worth trusting Android Police's Marvin Velasco tested four to five free apps in each category on a single ARCore-compatible Android phone and found the honest split: a bubble level running off the gyroscope and accelerometer worked perfectly fine and could be calibrated, and a magnetometer-based digital compass pointed true without any calibration at all, while AR measuring apps came in off by an inch or two with inconsistent repeats, a light meter was awkward to position, and a guitar tuner lagged and missed; the thermometer and elevation apps were the clear failures, since a phone has no temperature sensor to read and the altitude figure simply came back wrong.
needs: An Android phone with a gyroscope
A real ruler to check against

workflows.title: Turn the Windows PC that is already online into the Wi-Fi hotspot the room needs
workflows.dek: One buried toggle XDA's Hamlin Rozario finds Mobile hotspot on the second page of the Windows 11 Quick Settings panel, or under Settings, Network and internet, Mobile hotspot, then right-clicks the tile and picks Go to settings to name the network, set a password, and choose the 2.4GHz or 5GHz band, which matters because leaving it on any available can hide the hotspot from older devices that only speak 2.4GHz; he is straight that a motherboard adapter will not match a real router for range, and that everything connected drops when the PC restarts.
needs: A Windows 11 PC with a Wi-Fi adapter

workflows.title: Write the whole card before you trust it, and a counterfeit SD card gives itself away
workflows.dek: Fill it, then read it back How-To Geek's Nick Lewis backs up anything already on a new card, reformats it as exFAT, points the H2testw utility at the drive, selects all available space, and lets it write test files across the whole card and read every one of them back, which is how a card claiming capacity it does not have finally admits it; he warns that a large slow card can take hours and must not be interrupted, that sustained speeds below the advertised peak are normal, and that buying from an authorized retailer is no guarantee, since counterfeits turn up in returned stock.
needs: A Windows PC to run H2testw
A new card with nothing left on it
Hours you can leave it running

workflows.title: Practice the Excel functions you actually need on data you enjoy arguing about
workflows.dek: Four projects, real functions How-To Geek's Jorge A. Aguilar learns Excel on Pokemon data pulled free from Bulbapedia, building a dashboard from named Excel Tables and PivotTables, an odds simulator that runs thousands of random trials through Data Tables and RAND, a calculator that leans on INT, ROUNDDOWN, MAX, and MIN against a lookup table of parameters, and a synergy grid assembled from XLOOKUP, SUMPRODUCT, and conditional formatting; the functions are the same ones a budget or a sales report needs, and he flags the two traps, since RAND recalculates the entire workbook on any edit and scattered formatting rules bloat the file until you consolidate them in Rules Manager.
needs: An evening for the first project

workflows.title: Set Google Meet's audio and framing once so the first five minutes of a call stop being a sound check
workflows.dek: Audio first, camera second Android Police's Kabir Jain switches on Settings, Audio, Studio sound so the microphone drops everything that is not speech, adds Settings, Audio, Push to talk to hold the spacebar to unmute, turns on Backgrounds and effects, Appearance, Framing to stay centered in the shot, raises or lowers Settings, Video, Send resolution and Receive resolution to match the connection he actually has, and sets Settings, General, Leave empty calls so a meeting nobody joins does not sit open behind him.
needs: Five minutes before a real call

workflows.title: Hand Gemini's extensions and scheduled actions the recurring jobs thirteen separate apps were doing
workflows.dek: One assistant, thirteen apps Android Police's Jade Bryan Jardinico enables the Calendar, Keep, and Tasks extensions, sets up Gemini Spark as an email agent with written instructions, builds scheduled actions for recurring work such as a news briefing, keeps separate chat sessions for fitness tracking and meal planning, and connects his smart home through Google Home, retiring roughly thirteen apps including Microsoft To Do, Todoist, and MyFitnessPal; standard scheduled actions run without a paid plan, though Spark's advanced abilities need Pro or Ultra, and the work is mostly a couple of minutes spent sharpening the prompts.
needs: A few minutes to refine prompts

workflows.title: Open one Obsidian daily note each morning and let the built-in plugin build the page for you
workflows.dek: One note, every morning Android Police's Marvin Velasco turns on the built-in Daily Notes core plugin, points it at a template file, puts the code {{date:dddd, MMMM D}} at the top so each day names itself, adds an Ongoing Projects section that links out to the notes that matter, and drops the Daily Notes widget on his Android home screen so one tap opens an editable page for today; he deliberately stripped the other plugins back out, writing that doing less with Obsidian made him more productive.

workflows.title: Seven Kindle tweaks that turn a cluttered library into a shelf you can actually read from
workflows.dek: Group, sort, filter, prune Android Police's Jesse Hollington collapses long series under Settings, Home and Library, Group Series in Library, moves the Sort button's View Options to List and then to Collections, sets the Filter button to Downloaded and Unread so the choice survives a restart, builds collections around what he is doing rather than genre (In Progress, Up Next, Reference) and marks them Favorites, bulk-deletes sample books from the web dashboard at amazon.com/myk, and fills in title, author, and cover art on sideloaded files with the free Calibre before sending them across.
needs: A Kindle or the Kindle app

workflows.title: Set your 2.4GHz Wi-Fi to channel 1, 6, or 11 by hand and stop it overlapping the neighbors
workflows.dek: Three channels, no overlap Gavin Phillips explains that the 2.4GHz band holds 83.5MHz of usable spectrum cut into 11 channels spaced 5MHz apart while each channel is about 22MHz wide, so only 1, 6, and 11 avoid stepping on each other: run a Wi-Fi analyzer in the evening when the building is busiest, pick the quietest of the three in your router's settings instead of leaving it on automatic, move whatever devices you can to 5GHz or 6GHz, and rescan now and then, because in a dense area you can still end up sharing a channel.
needs: An evening scan, not a morning one

workflows.title: Six Windows 11 habits that give back a few minutes a day, starting with one update command
workflows.dek: Six switches and shortcuts Pankil Shah updates every Winget-installed program at once by running winget upgrade -all in Command Prompt, turns on Settings, System, Advanced, End task so a frozen window can be closed straight from the taskbar, opens unknown software inside Windows Sandbox where everything is deleted on exit, mirrors an Android screen through Phone Link, remaps three and four finger touchpad gestures, and keeps Win+V clipboard history and Win+. emoji within reach; two limits are worth knowing, since Sandbox needs Windows 11 Pro and the Winget command leaves Microsoft Store apps alone.

workflows.title: Read the Google Maps traffic layer before you pull out of the driveway, not just the ETA
workflows.dek: Look before you drive Parth Shah taps the map icon on the Google Maps home screen, chooses Traffic under Map details, and reads the color-coded roads around the trip, spotting the red and dark red stretches before navigation begins rather than trusting a single estimated arrival time, then taps the three dot menu after entering directions to set a departure or arrival time and see how the drive should look later; he is honest that the habit pays best on routes you already know, because seeing the jam only helps if you know the way around it.

workflows.title: The five Android settings worth changing in the first ten minutes with a new phone
workflows.dek: Five switches, once How-To Geek's Sanya Shah hides notification contents on the lock screen under Settings, Notifications, Hide content while locked, narrows app location access to Ask every time or While using the app under Settings, Location, App permissions, turns off adaptive brightness under Display, switches off Ad topics and App-suggested ads under Security and Privacy, More privacy settings, Ads, and stops the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth scanning that continues even with both radios off under Location services; the piece is honest about what each one costs, since manual brightness means adjusting the screen yourself room by room, the ad change makes advertising more generic rather than making it disappear, and turning off scanning trims little battery while it does cost some location accuracy.

workflows.title: Empty the Windows 11 Start menu of everything Microsoft put there for you
workflows.dek: One clean launcher MakeUseOf's Oluwaseun Bamisile opens Settings, then Personalization, then Start, and turns off recently installed apps, most used apps, recommended files, the mobile device panel, and the recommendations for tips, shortcuts, and new apps, controls that recent Windows updates finally expose as switches where earlier versions offered none; the counterpoint comes from the author, who left the suggestions running for a couple of days first and found them genuinely helpful in rare cases, so anyone who reopens recent documents all day may want to keep that single one on.

workflows.title: Put the dates back in the Google Photos grid that the summer redesign took away
workflows.dek: Dates back in the grid Android Authority's Joe Maring restores the date markers that Google's July 2026 redesign removed from the Photos home screen: tap the profile icon, then Photos settings, then Preferences, then Photos view, then switch on Show dates in grid, an option that ships turned off and sits several menus down; the fix is partial by the author's own account, since a floating date pill still rides at the top of the screen as you scroll, and the redesign is described as form over function that made the app more cumbersome to use.

workflows.title: Four Waze settings that stop the app from routing you down an alley to save a minute
workflows.dek: Four settings, calmer routes Android Police's Jade Bryan Jardinico sets Avoid difficult intersections to Always under Settings, Navigation, matches the active vehicle profile to the car actually being driven, adjusts the unpaved road preference in the same Navigation settings, and anchors a route by tapping the ETA bar to add a waypoint so crowdsourced traffic data cannot pull the trip through a narrow alley mid-drive; the article does not oversell the result, granting that some of Waze's rerouting suggestions really are helpful and that the algorithm is far from perfect, with the approach working best for city driving and long road trips.

workflows.title: Five tiny AutoHotkey scripts that take the repeated clicks out of a Windows day
workflows.dek: Five short scripts Tony Phillips uses AutoHotkey v2.0, free and open source for Windows, to bind Ctrl+Alt+W to open a set of sites at once, Ctrl+Alt+D to create and open a folder named for today's date, Ctrl+Shift+G to search whatever text is highlighted, a short code such as eaddr to expand into a full address, and Ctrl+Alt+T to keep a window on top of the others; he warns that the search script replaces whatever is already on the Windows clipboard, so do not fire it while you are holding something you need.

workflows.title: Put related Excel tables into the Data Model and stop maintaining lookup formulas
workflows.dek: One workbook, real relationships Yasir Mahmood describes Excel's Data Model as a compressed relational store held inside the workbook itself: tick Add this data to the Data Model when you build a PivotTable, drag matching keys onto each other in Power Pivot's Diagram View, and a single PivotTable can then reach every related table through the Field List, with DAX measures for the harder calculations; he is candid that these relationships are not database-enforced, that the join fields have to share a data type, and that past a certain size a spreadsheet buckles as a system of record.
needs: A shared key column in each

workflows.title: Put the forgotten USB port on your router to work as shared storage, a print server, or a backup line
workflows.dek: Five jobs, one port Afam Onyimadu walks through turning a router's USB port into network storage every device in the house can reach, a print server for a single USB printer, a cellular failover line using a tethered phone or USB modem, remote file access over FTP with optional DDNS, and a DLNA media server for the TV; he is straight about the limits, since support varies by manufacturer and printer compatibility is especially patchy, permissions and redundancy fall well short of a real NAS, and remote FTP needs secure sharing turned on rather than anonymous access.
needs: A router with a USB port
A USB drive, printer, or modem

workflows.title: Four Android Auto settings that keep your hands off the phone for the whole drive
workflows.dek: Set once, every drive Patrick O'Rourke sets Android Auto to start Always rather than only if it was used on the last drive, turns on automatic music playback so nothing needs tapping on the way out of the driveway, enables Silence Notifications While Driving under Safety and Emergency so Bluetooth and motion detection trigger it, and moves the media controls nearer the driver under Change Layout; the tradeoff he names is real, because bringing media within reach pushes Google Maps and Waze to the far side of the screen, and he calls Gemini's voice responses frustratingly unreliable.

workflows.title: Stop swiping apps closed, and restrict only the few that actually misbehave in the background
workflows.dek: Restrict, do not swipe Brandon Miniman makes the case that clearing the recents list forces a cold start that spikes the processor to nearly 100 percent, where waking an app from hibernation spikes it to about 50 percent, so on a modern phone, which he says should carry at least 8GB of RAM, he leaves apps alone and instead opens Settings, then Apps, then the offender, then Battery (Restricted on Samsung Galaxy phones), and turns off background usage for that one app; he warns plainly that a restricted app may misbehave or drop notifications, and he still swipes away anything frozen or glitching.
needs: A short list of suspect apps

workflows.title: Move your notes into a plain Markdown folder and let Syncthing carry it between your devices
workflows.dek: One folder, no database Anurag Singh left Notion for ordinary .md files in a regular folder, with subfolders only where he wants them, edited in VSCode or an alternative like Cursor, Antigravity, Zed, or Neovim, then installed Syncthing on each device, paired them by device ID, and shared that one folder so a change on one machine lands on the others; he is candid about the limits, since Syncthing synchronizes rather than backs up, a deletion travels to every device, and editing the same file on two devices that are out of contact leaves you with a conflict copy.
needs: A text editor you already like
One folder to hold the .md files
A separate backup of that folder

workflows.title: Clean four things in the raw data before you build the PivotTable that has to read it
workflows.dek: Enrich, classify, split, trim Tony Phillips runs a sales table through four functions before any PivotTable exists: XLOOKUP pulls product names and categories in from a second table, IF turns transaction amounts into High Value and Standard labels, TEXTSPLIT breaks a combined Chicago | IL | Midwest field into city, state, and region columns, and TRIM strips the stray spaces that would otherwise scatter one customer across several rows.
needs: A raw data sheet to tidy
A lookup table of product details

workflows.title: Set up Chrome's own remote desktop for the five-minute job you left on the other computer
workflows.dek: One code, or a PIN Afam Onyimadu sets up Chrome Remote Desktop two ways, a one-time access code for a quick share and a registered host with a PIN for passwordless return visits, and he is straight about the cost: the host has to stay powered on, online, and out of sleep, which drains a laptop battery and raises CPU temperatures, so he keeps it for grabbing a forgotten file rather than a full day of remote work.
needs: Hands-on setup at the host PC
The host left awake and online

workflows.title: Reclaim Android storage with the four tools already on the phone instead of a cleaner app
workflows.dek: Clean, trash, photos, cache Goran Damnjanovic drops the third-party cleaner apps for four things already installed: the Clean tab in Files by Google or Samsung's My Files, the trash folder most people never empty, Free Up Space On This Device in Google Photos, and clearing individual app caches under Settings, Storage, Apps, which together freed about 23GB in his own testing.
needs: Files by Google or Samsung My Files

workflows.title: Four free DNS services, each better at one job than Google's or Cloudflare's
workflows.dek: Pick by the problem Pankil Shah lines up AdGuard DNS for stopping ads and trackers at the lookup itself, Quad9 for malware and phishing, screened against threat intelligence from more than 20 cybersecurity organizations by a Swiss nonprofit that promises to collect no user data, CleanBrowsing for households that want adult content blocked and SafeSearch forced on, and Mullvad's dns.mullvad.net, a strict no-logs resolver offered in adblock, base, extended, family, and all-in-one variants; he is straight about the tradeoffs, since AdGuard cannot touch ads served from the same domain as the page and needs its paid app for ads inside other apps, and CleanBrowsing's filtering is blunt enough to catch legitimate sites while whitelisting stays on the paid plans.
needs: Your router or device DNS settings
One device to test on first

workflows.title: Five Android safety settings that ask for help when you cannot
workflows.dek: Set up the check-in first Roydon Cerejo starts in Google's Personal Safety app, where Safety Check asks you to confirm you are fine after a set time and, if you never answer, tells your emergency contacts your last known location, and can also alert them when the battery falls below 15 percent; from there he turns on Emergency SOS, which triggers on five or more rapid presses of the power button on Android 13 and later and can record a clip to the cloud, Car Crash Detection on a Pixel 4a or newer, Digital Wellbeing's Heads Up nudge for people who scroll while walking, and screen time reminders that appear after 15 to 20 minutes in one app; he does not oversell any of it, calling Heads Up wildly inconsistent across several phones and noting that Safety Check has no home screen widget.

workflows.title: Turn a webcam and two desk lamps into a document scanner that makes real PDFs
workflows.dek: Square the camera first Jorge A. Aguilar mounts a webcam, 4K if you have one and 1080p if you do not, on a copy stand, a heavy desk clamp, or a rigid mini tripod, sets the lens at 90 degrees and parallel to the page, locks manual focus where the camera allows it, and lights the paper with two lamps so one side is not brighter than the other, then lets Camscan, a free MIT-licensed app with Windows and Linux builds, find the page edges in the live video, reorder, rotate, or drop pages, and export the batch as one PDF; he says plainly that a webcam scanner is not going to match a flatbed on every job, and that the more complicated scans, photographs and fine print, are not going to look amazing.
needs: A copy stand, clamp, or tripod

workflows.title: Six router changes that fix slow Wi-Fi before you spend anything on new hardware
workflows.dek: Placement first, then bands Monica J. White moves the router to a central, elevated spot outside a closed cabinet and tests the weak rooms before and after, assigns undemanding devices to 2.4GHz and speed-sensitive ones to 5GHz instead of trusting automatic band steering, narrows the 2.4GHz channel width to 20MHz for stability, splits the two bands into separate network names rather than one Smart Connect SSID, and turns off DFS channels or pins 5GHz to channels 36 to 48 or 149 to 165 for homes near an airport, coastline, or weather radar; the piece warns never to disable 2.4GHz entirely, since some devices need its longer range, and notes that some ISP-supplied routers will not allow a firmware update at all.
needs: One room that drops the signal

workflows.title: Turn off the two background scanners that quietly drain an Android phone overnight
workflows.dek: Two switches under Location Robin John turns off Wi-Fi scanning and Bluetooth scanning under Settings, Location, Location services on a Pixel, where Samsung's One UI keeps them in the same place, and reports overnight drain falling from around five or six percent to closer to three over two weeks; the cost is real, because Find Hub depends on those scanners to track devices and indoor accuracy suffers enough that Google Maps landed on the wrong side of a building and ride-hailing apps took longer to pin down a pickup, so the piece suggests turning off Wi-Fi scanning alone if you pair new accessories often.
needs: Two weeks to judge the result

workflows.title: Seven built-in camera tools that copy text off paper and build multipage PDFs
workflows.dek: Point, then copy the text Jade Bryan Jardinico stays inside tools the phone already has: the Samsung camera's text button lifts words straight off a page to paste elsewhere, the Scan toggle turns detected paper borders into a multipage PDF with Add Scan, Google Drive does the scanning job on a Pixel, and Bixby Vision reads printed text aloud or names a color at a stated 85 to 90 percent accuracy; the write-up is candid that multi-column layouts and irregular typography make the text capture miss lines, so reframe and work in smaller batches, that low light throws the color reading off, and that several of the seven are Samsung One UI features with a Google Drive or Gemini workaround elsewhere.
needs: Google Drive or Samsung One UI

workflows.title: Find the hidden bloat that makes an Excel workbook take forever to open
workflows.dek: Ctrl+End tells the truth Tony Phillips presses Ctrl+End to see where Excel thinks the data ends and deletes the empty rows and columns beyond it, clears obsolete defined names and broken external links out of Formulas, Name Manager, hunts down volatile functions such as NOW, TODAY, RAND, OFFSET, and INDIRECT, checks Data, Queries and Connections for links nobody uses, and renames a copy of the .xlsx to .zip to look inside xl/media for oversized embedded images; he warns you to back up first, to confirm nothing you delete is referenced by a formula, chart, or macro, and that the zip inspection does not work on binary .xlsb files.
needs: A backup copy of the workbook

workflows.title: Three Chrome privacy switches, and a plain account of what they still cannot do for you
workflows.dek: Cookies, location, then HTTPS Oluwaseun Bamisile blocks third-party cookies under Settings, Privacy and security, sets Site settings, Location to the option that stops sites seeing where you are, and turns on Always use secure connections under Security, then says outright what none of it accomplishes: it cannot hide an IP address, cannot match what a VPN gives you on an untrusted network, and cannot stop tracking that follows your accounts, your device habits, or the location inferred from your IP alone.

workflows.title: Nine commands that tell you where a Windows internet problem actually is before you call anyone
workflows.dek: Ping outward, one step at a time Pankil Shah works from the router out: ping 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1 to prove the router answers, ping 8.8.8.8 to skip DNS entirely, ping google.com to test name resolution, then nslookup google.com and nslookup google.com 8.8.8.8 to see whether your own DNS server is the fault, ipconfig /flushdns to clear a bad cache, and tracert google.com to find where the delay begins; netsh winsock reset and netsh int ip reset come last and want a restart afterward, and none of it repairs failed hardware or an ISP outage.

workflows.title: Let Windows empty its own temp files, Recycle Bin, and stale downloads on a schedule you choose
workflows.dek: Storage Sense, switched on Settings, then System, then Storage turns on automatic user content cleanup, which clears the Recycle Bin after 30 days by default and can put the Downloads folder, which otherwise never deletes anything, on a 1, 14, 30, or 60 day timer.

workflows.title: Trade a slice of your top speed for video calls that stop freezing for everyone in the house
workflows.dek: Quality of Service, deliberately XDA's Ty Sherback turned on QoS in a TP-Link Archer router, entered the real upload and download figures from the ISP, set priority percentages, and flagged the devices that matter, accepting a lower ceiling because QoS drops the router into software forwarding that consumer silicon cannot push gigabit traffic through.
needs: A router with a QoS setting
Your ISP's real up and down speeds
A bufferbloat test, before and after

workflows.title: Turn on the taskbar right-click that force-quits a frozen app without opening Task Manager
workflows.dek: One toggle, then every taskbar Windows 11 hides an End Task switch under Settings, System, Advanced (For developers on some builds), and How-To Geek's Tony Phillips is clear about the cost: it kills the process outright rather than asking it to close, it takes every window of that app at once, and unsaved work goes with it.

workflows.title: Four prompts that turn Claude from an explainer into flashcards, diagrams, and simulations you study with
workflows.dek: Build it, do not read it Abhijith N Arjunan asks for an interactive flashcard deck that self-grades and resurfaces every card you miss before the session ends, a step-through diagram that moves one stage at a time rather than arriving as a single static image, and a slider-driven simulation you can drag to watch one variable change the outcome in real time, then leans on Claude's /learn skill to shape the language for learning; he warns that the step-through diagrams cost more tokens and time than the flashcards, and that concern over source fidelity sends him elsewhere for video and audio material.
needs: A subject you are trying to learn
The four prompts from the piece

workflows.title: Collapse a scattered task system into one Google Keep note with dated and themed sections
workflows.dek: One note, many sections Andy Walker dumps practically everything that crosses his mind into a single Keep note, then splits the task half into recurring work, what is due this month, what is due this week, and a line for each weekday kept a week ahead, moves anything unfinished into the section where it now belongs instead of reshuffling the whole list, and keeps a block for undated jobs plus themed dumps for car maintenance, meal planning, research ideas, and finances; he concedes the note has no alarms or integrations, needs daily discipline, and sends anything heavier to Notion, Samsung Food, or Raindrop.io.
needs: Google Keep on phone or web
Ten minutes to lay out sections
A daily habit of updating it

workflows.title: Export a spreadsheet to CSV and have an AI assistant hand back a single-file app that works offline
workflows.dek: CSV first, then prompt Tony Phillips exports the workbook as CSV so the formatting and formulas fall away and only the fields remain, here 5,000 personal finance transactions carrying id, date, amount, description, category, budget group, account name, and account type, then hands the identical request to Gemini, Claude, and Copilot: one HTML file with search, filtering, sorting, pagination, add, edit and delete, summary dashboards, and data that persists locally; Gemini and Claude both returned working apps and Copilot did not, and neither working app handled filters that depend on one another.
needs: An AI assistant, Gemini or Claude
A web browser to open the file

workflows.title: Find out what is actually slowing a Windows PC before you buy anything to fix it
workflows.dek: Measure, then fix Tashreef Shareef starts with AppControl, which keeps seven days of CPU, GPU, memory, disk, and temperature history so yesterday's slowdown can still be traced to its cause, then uses Wintoys to review apps, background services, system tweaks, and storage cleanup from one window, CrystalDiskMark to settle whether the drive is the bottleneck with sequential and random 4K tests, and Microsoft PC Manager for the plain work of clearing temporary files and uninstalling leftovers; all four are free, and the piece flags that Wintoys is closed source and that its developer has mentioned future paid premium features, none of which have appeared yet.

workflows.title: Cut a 300-a-day notification pile down to the alerts you actually want
workflows.dek: Five passes, one system Vishwamoorthy Ramakrishnan turns notifications off outright for rarely opened apps by long-pressing the icon and going through App Info to Notifications, then splits the apps worth keeping into their own categories so an order update arrives and the promotion behind it does not, gives the categories that matter distinct sounds so the phone can be read without looking at it, switches on the snooze button to push an alert up to two hours out, and enables notification history to recover anything swiped away in the last 24 hours; the warning attached is that snoozing and history are off by default and sit behind differently named menus on Pixel and Samsung phones.

workflows.title: Build a one-tap travel mode on a Samsung Galaxy so the phone changes its own rules
workflows.dek: Set once, reuse always T.M. Amrita opens Settings, then Modes and Routines, adds a custom mode, and decides inside it which apps and notifications get through, what the display does, and how do not disturb behaves, optionally attaching if-then routines so the mode switches itself on, then puts it on the home screen or in the notification panel so one tap flips the whole phone into it; the setup happens once and is reused every trip, and Amrita notes newer Galaxy models label the feature differently and that phones without it need a third-party automation app such as IFTTT.
needs: A home screen or panel slot

workflows.title: Five habits that turn a Gemini Notebook study guide from a generic summary into something you can study from
workflows.dek: Sources first Saikat Basu keeps one notebook per topic rather than one pile, unchecks the sources that do not belong before generating anything, states who is asking (student, researcher, casual learner) so the guide aims at the right depth, then refuses the first draft and chains follow-ups such as identify the top three most complex concepts; he previews the raw extracted text to catch OCR damage before it reaches the model and clicks through citations to check them, warning that subtle nuance in legal, medical, or technical material gets lost in paraphrase.

workflows.title: Five prompts that reshape a finished research report into a website, a chart set, a slide deck, or a designed PDF
workflows.dek: One report, five shapes Abhijith N Arjunan hands a finished text report back to Claude with one prompt per format: a single HTML page with fixed navigation and tabbed themes, a set of bar and line charts built with Recharts plus dashboard tiles for standalone numbers, a draggable force-directed concept graph in the Obsidian style, a full-screen slide deck you move through with arrow keys, and a PDF with a cover page, section dividers, and pull-quote callouts; he is upfront that each format still asks for time on what its design demands.
needs: Some HTML comfort to adjust output

workflows.title: Stop the ISP box and your own router from fighting by putting one of them in bridge mode
workflows.dek: One router in charge Oliver Haslam explains that leaving both boxes routing gives you two DHCP servers handing out duplicate addresses, two firewalls, competing Wi-Fi networks, and double NAT, which he says can make it impossible for devices to connect to online services; his preferred fix is bridge mode, sometimes labeled modem mode, which switches off the ISP box's routing, Wi-Fi, and firewall and leaves the modem doing modem work, with a DMZ plus a static IP or access point mode as fallbacks, and he notes that not every ISP router offers bridge mode because some providers disable it to keep support simple.

workflows.title: Plan the trip on a laptop, then hand the finished route to the phone you will navigate with
workflows.dek: Big screen first Andy Betts drags points on a desktop route to build his own detours, drops a pin and uses the travel time tool to see everywhere within a set walking or driving distance, saves restaurants and stops into lists while he researches, and keeps several tabs open to compare alternate routes and times together, then sends the finished route to his phone with a button or a shareable link, and he notes the whole handoff rests on the account syncing between the two devices.
needs: One Google account on both devices

workflows.title: Six settings changes that make an aging Windows PC feel quicker without buying any hardware
workflows.dek: Six free toggles Goran Damnjanovic switches off animation effects under Settings, Accessibility, Visual effects, clears programs out of Settings, Apps, Startup, debloats with a utility such as Chris Titus' WinUtil or simply removes Copilot, which he says can use around 500MB of RAM in the background, disables services an underpowered machine does not need, sets the power mode to best performance, and turns off online Bing results in Windows Search; he is candid that older and weaker PCs gain far more from all of this than new ones, and that best performance runs hotter and shortens battery life.

workflows.title: Write the rules once and let the Downloads folder file itself by type, year, and month
workflows.dek: If this, then filed Tashreef Shareef points File Juggler at his Downloads folder and writes each rule as a plain condition and action, if the extension is .pdf, then move the file, then uses date variables so the destination builds its own year and month subfolders, ending with more than five rules covering PDFs, images, installers, archives, and Markdown files; the program can also match on filename patterns, file size, modification date, and keywords inside a document, and MakeUseOf puts the cost at a $40 perpetual license after a 30 day trial that keeps working with upgrade popups.
needs: File Juggler, $40 after a 30 day trial

workflows.title: Move the router off the floor and away from the fridge before you buy a new one
workflows.dek: Height beats hardware Samarveer Singh had already split the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands and let his provider's app pick channels, yet a laptop pulling the full 300 Mbps over a cable managed only about 50 Mbps over Wi-Fi, so he took the router off a three foot chest standing beside the refrigerator and put it on a wall shelf up near the ceiling, which left every room a single wall's thickness from the signal and steadied televisions that had been struggling, and he is careful to say placement is one of three factors alongside the hardware itself and its settings.
needs: A higher spot away from metal
A speed test before and after

workflows.title: Turn off three Samsung settings and the keyboard stops feeling a half step behind you
workflows.dek: Three toggles, one keyboard Brandon Miniman opens the keyboard's settings cog and switches off Character preview and Vibration under Swipe, touch and feedback, Touch feedback, then unlocks Developer Options by tapping Build number seven times under Settings, About phone, Software information and drops Window animation scale, Transition animation scale, and Animator duration scale to 0.5x, and he is candid that typing still does not match Gboard on a Pixel or the iOS keyboard.
needs: Developer Options, for the third step

workflows.title: Turn off four Android Auto defaults so the car stops blasting music and reading your texts to the passenger seat
workflows.dek: Four toggles, one drive Jorge A. Aguilar switches off Start music automatically under Settings, Android Auto, General, so plugging in stops greeting him with whatever was playing last at full volume, turns off Show first line of messages and Play AI message summaries under Connected devices, Android Auto, Messaging, because nobody wants a personal or embarrassing text suddenly splashed across the dashboard, moves Day and Night mode for maps from Automatic to Day in the Android Auto app after the system got stuck in night mode so dark the navigation map was basically unreadable, and raises the Speech rate slider under Settings, Accessibility, Text to speech output, since Google's engine ships at a pretty slow speaking rate, and he is careful to add that these defaults are not wrong for everyone.
needs: An Android phone with Android Auto

workflows.title: Sort a backlog of saved articles into act now, reference, archive, and delete in a single pass
workflows.dek: Four buckets, one pass Saikat Basu points Claude Desktop at his Obsidian folder through its filesystem connector, has it read all 500 clips at once instead of one at a time, sorts them into Act now, Reference, Archive, and Delete by weighing each clip against his current project notes, asks what themes run across the whole collection, and finds 50 worth keeping, then spends about fifteen minutes reading the result himself before anything moves, which is where he plants the warnings: the sort was a first pass, not a final answer, outdated or loosely defined project notes will make Claude hallucinate current relevance, code snippets, quick recipes, and single paragraph quotes can look like low value to an AI sorter, and his own review caught a clip wrongly marked a duplicate.
needs: An Obsidian vault of saved clips

workflows.title: Replace six utility downloads with tools Windows 11 already installed for you
workflows.dek: Six shortcuts, no installs Afam Onyimadu stopped downloading utilities once he worked through what ships in the box: Storage Sense under Settings, System, Storage in place of CCleaner, clipboard history on Win plus V in place of Ditto, Win plus Shift plus S for a screenshot and Win plus Shift plus R for a screen recording in place of ShareX, virtual desktops on Windows plus Ctrl plus an arrow key in place of VirtuaWin, Phone Link for notifications, messages, and file transfers in place of Pushbullet, and Quick Assist with its annotation, laser pointer, and chat for helping someone you already trust in place of TeamViewer, and he is candid about the edges: Storage Sense leans on OneDrive to make old files online only and clears only what Windows counts as safe, clipboard entries disappear at reboot unless you pin them, Phone Link features vary by Android model, and Quick Assist suits known contacts rather than a service left running in the background.
needs: Ten minutes to learn the shortcuts
An Android phone, for Phone Link

workflows.title: Format every spreadsheet the same way with five Excel tools you set up once
workflows.dek: Define it once, reuse it Tony Phillips builds named cell styles for input, calculation, and output cells under Home, Cell Styles, New Cell Style, then carries the whole set into the next workbook with Merge Styles, lets Conditional Formatting react to the data through data bars, icon sets, color scales, or a formula rule, sets figures with the Accounting, Percent, and Comma buttons in the Number group, writes custom formats under Ctrl plus 1, Number, Custom so a value can read as millions or show a dash instead of a zero without the number underneath changing, and switches off banded rows in Table Design when the stripes fight the color rules already on the sheet, and he attaches his own warnings: the original cell still has to be formatted by hand before a style can be built from it, and conditional formatting treated as decoration makes a sheet harder to read rather than clearer.
needs: Ctrl plus 1 for the format dialog

workflows.title: Turn a spare computer into a private photo library your phone backs itself up to
workflows.dek: Docker, then six commands Jack Mitchell installs Docker Desktop on a spare Mac, PC, or Linux machine, makes an immich-app folder, pulls the project's docker-compose.yml and example environment file with curl, edits that file to point at the disk where the photos and the database should live, brings the whole stack up with docker compose up in detached mode, then opens the library in a browser at localhost port 2283, registers, and installs the Immich phone app so the camera roll backs itself up to hardware he owns, with timeline views, albums, sharing, face recognition, and map data waiting there, and he does not oversell it: he calls Immich familiar and simple to use but not as automated or as feature rich as Google Photos, and the sharper limit comes from a reader underneath the piece, that sharing an album with someone outside the house means exposing the server beyond the home network, a security problem the average household is not equipped to handle.
needs: A spare Mac, PC, or Linux machine

workflows.title: Turn a course syllabus into a working study plan before the term starts
workflows.dek: One Collection per course Nolen Jonker sets up a Collection for each course before classes begin, adds the syllabus, readings, and lecture videos as separate threads that keep the source on one side and a chat panel on the other, has the syllabus thread pull out every deadline and graded component, writes his own weekly priorities next to that breakdown, and keeps one reference Collection for material that crosses courses, and he names the limits plainly: Gistr's free tier gives a full workspace with 300 AI credits a day before the paid plans he reports starting at $8 a month with a 50 percent student discount, video support covers YouTube rather than files you upload, and answers stay grounded in the sources you added unless you turn on web search.
needs: A free Gistr account in the browser
Your syllabus and readings as files

workflows.title: Keep one USB drive that can boot, repair, and scan any Windows PC in the house
workflows.dek: Ventoy, then drag and drop Ismar Hrnjicevic installs the free Ventoy2Disk utility onto a 64GB EAGET dual connector drive he bought for $16, then simply copies in the files he wants to boot from, a Windows 11 ISO, Hiren's BootCD PE for a live desktop, Malwarebytes for cleanup, and HWiNFO for hardware readings, and uses Ventoy's Preserve space option so a second FAT32 partition made in Disk Management can still carry ordinary files, and he does not oversell the hardware: the drive runs hot enough under sustained use to slow itself down, its small connectors and exposed ports want caps and care, and he keeps an electric duster nearby for cooling.
needs: The ISOs and tools you want aboard

workflows.title: Replace six separate apps with one browser's built-in mail, calendar, notes, and screenshot tools
workflows.dek: One window, six jobs Shaheer Khan moved his browsing, note-taking, screenshots, email, calendar, and YouTube into Vivaldi, stacking and tiling tabs to keep related pages together, separating contexts with workspaces, writing in the markdown notepad, and running the built-in mail and calendar clients, and he is candid about the cost of it: Vivaldi will give a machine with less memory a run for its money, and the browser felt overwhelming to him at first even though it can import your Chrome or Edge data.
needs: Your Chrome or Edge data to import

workflows.title: Pick one clear Wi-Fi channel by hand instead of letting the router choose it for you
workflows.dek: Analyzer first, then lock Oluwaseun Bamisile checked the networks around him with a Wi-Fi analyzer app, then replaced his router's automatic channel selection with a fixed one, settling on channel 6 because 1, 6, and 11 are the only non-overlapping channels on 2.4GHz, and naming 36, 40, 44, and 48 as the best starting points on 5GHz, and he says his connection became more stable without claiming a number for it, adding that the picks are not set in stone: the right channel depends on your region and the congestion nearby, and which channels a router may legally use depends on your country, so its region setting has to be correct.

workflows.title: Let a Samsung phone quiet itself, stretch its battery, and call out the time you lose to YouTube
workflows.dek: Settings, Modes and Routines Zunaid Ali builds routines that switch on Do Not Disturb, power saving, and grayscale between midnight and 5 AM, run a thirty-minute nap timer that reads a message aloud, and tighten battery saving in two steps, first at 50 percent and again at 30 percent with data saver and dimmed brightness, then adds a Gmail filter on the desktop site that keeps chosen senders out of Spam and in Primary, and one loop in the free Automate app that tells him how long he has actually been sitting on YouTube; he estimates the set saves him about thirty minutes a day, and he grants that the schedules need adjusting every few months and that a nap timer cannot ring a real alarm sound.

workflows.title: Name every range in a spreadsheet at once with Ctrl+Shift+F3 instead of typing them one by one
workflows.dek: Create Names from Selection Tony Phillips selects the labels along with the data they describe, presses Ctrl+Shift+F3, and Excel writes a named range for every label in a few seconds, and he names the catches: a blank row between the labels and the data stops it, duplicate labels fail, spaces in a label become underscores, and formulas you already wrote keep their cell references until you run Apply Names.
needs: Excel with labels next to the data

workflows.title: Replace a paid remote-desktop subscription with self-hosted RustDesk and Tailscale
workflows.dek: Docker, then Tailscale Tashreef Shareef deploys the open-source RustDesk server in Docker containers, installs the free clients on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android, then layers Tailscale on top so he can reach his home PC from a coffee shop, a hotel, or a phone hotspot without opening a single port on his router, and he is straight about the catches: self-hosted RustDesk on its own only works inside your local network, and the setup is fairly quick only if you are already comfortable with Docker.
needs: Docker Desktop on the host PC

workflows.title: Turn off what your Android keyboard remembers, or swap it for one that keeps everything on the phone
workflows.dek: Settings, then Privacy Tashreef Shareef switches off usage-statistics sharing in Gboard's Privacy settings and in the Smart typing section of Samsung Keyboard, clears the stored data with the reset option, and revokes the contacts, camera, and microphone permissions, then offers LeanType, HeliBoard, FUTO Keyboard, and AnySoftKeyboard as on-device alternatives, while granting that they can mean sideloading an APK and predictions that are less sharp than the mainstream option.

workflows.title: Turn the file copies you have been calling backups into snapshots you can actually restore
workflows.dek: Snapshots, not copies Afam Onyimadu realized that his external drive, his cloud sync folder, and his internal drive all held the same current version of every file, so deleting or overwriting one wiped all three at once, and he replaced the habit with restic, a free and open-source backup program he installed on Windows with scoop install restic, which stores timestamped snapshots you can restore from a chosen date and can verify its own integrity, and he is candid that it is a command-line tool with a real learning curve and that you have to test a restore on another device before you trust it.
needs: restic, free on Win, Mac, Linux
A storage destination, local or cloud

workflows.title: Feed a year of Kindle highlights into Gemini Notebook and get a searchable reading archive
workflows.dek: Start with My Clippings Saikat Basu pulls the My Clippings.txt file off the Kindle, optionally strips the metadata in a text editor, uploads it to Gemini Notebook as a source, and then asks it for the themes running across books, a commonplace book for a writing project, and citations back to the original titles, and he names the catches: the notebook will sometimes force a connection between unrelated highlights, attributions need checking by hand, there is no Readwise-style daily reminder email, and adopting a generated summary verbatim is plagiarism waiting to happen.
needs: A Kindle and its My Clippings.txt

workflows.title: Make an aging Android phone feel new again without a factory reset
workflows.dek: Four fixes, no reset Ismar Hrnjicevic frees up storage, keeps Android and its apps updated, strips away widgets and the background activity of apps that abuse it, and replaces a tired battery, while warning that memory cleaner apps do more harm than good and that a phone can feel slower for a while after an update as it rebuilds app caches.
needs: A replacement battery if it is old

workflows.title: Build a live Excel dashboard with the Camera button hidden in the toolbar
workflows.dek: File, then Options Adaeze Uche adds the Camera command to the Quick Access Toolbar from the Commands Not in the Ribbon list, then snaps ranges off any sheet into one dashboard where every snapshot redraws itself as its source data changes, and she names the catches: it will not capture a chart object directly, the image degrades below about half size, and the live link does not survive a paste into another program.
needs: A workbook with a few sheets
Five minutes to add the button

workflows.title: Retire the Adobe subscription with four free apps for photos, video, design, and PDFs
